text:
The government confirms IRA-style tax incentive for growth strategy while critics warn benefits may favor large firms without cash support

Amid the global technological hegemony competition and supply chain restructuring, the government has finally confirmed the official introduction of the Domestic Production Tax Credit (Domestic Production Promotion Tax System), dubbed the ‘Korean Inflation Reduction Act (IRA).’

According to the ‘Economic Growth Strategy for the Second Half of 2026’ released by the government on July 20, the core premise is a tax benefit that directly reduces corporate tax and income tax in proportion to the volume when core strategic technology items are produced and sold domestically from the perspective of national security and eco-friendly green transition.

While the existing support system was a one-time benefit concentrated on the research and development (R&D) stage or the facility investment stage such as factory establishment, this system signifies a ‘supplier and production volume-linked’ paradigm shift that constantly reduces taxes whenever actual products are manufactured and sold. This is interpreted as a desperate measure to prevent the hollowing out of the domestic manufacturing industry in a situation where major countries such as the United States, Japan, and Europe are pouring out unprecedented cash subsidies and tax benefits to attract manufacturing bases within their own borders.

However, behind the market’s enthusiastic welcome, criticisms and limitations surrounding its effectiveness also clearly exist. This article diagnoses the light and shade of the Korean IRA system and the shockwaves it will cause on the domestic industrial ecosystem in the future.

Background and Core Contents of the Introduction of 'Korean IRA’

The protectionist barriers of major countries are rising day by day. The United States is drawing companies into its territory through the Advanced Manufacturing Production Credit (AMPC) of the IRA, while Japan has been implementing a production promotion policy since 2024 that provides tax support of 400,000 yen per 1 electric vehicle. The sense of crisis in the parts and finished vehicle industries that a massive overseas exodus of domestic high-tech industries and the collapse of the manufacturing base could become a reality has led to the government’s decisive action.

The newly established Domestic Production Tax Credit is expected to encompass about 10 national strategic technology sectors, covering semiconductors, secondary battery (battery) materials and parts, displays, biopharmaceuticals, and clean hydrogen, as well as finished vehicles and core automobile parts (electric and hydrogen vehicles). It is a structure in which the amount calculated by multiplying the domestically produced volume by the unit price per item set by the government is largely deducted from the corporate tax.

Institutional Limitations, Core Problems, and Supplementary Measures

The industry empathizes with the purpose of the system but is expressing disappointment that the core substance is missing. The biggest problem arising from the currently discussed structure is the absence of a ‘cash support measure’ and the resulting polarization of benefits among companies.

The core of the United States IRA is that it guarantees ‘Direct Pay,’ which allows even deficit-ridden companies with no immediate taxes to pay to receive tax credit amounts back in cash, or ‘Transferability,’ which allows companies to finance funds by selling their credit rights to third parties. On the other hand, the South Korean government’s draft remains limited to a method of deducting from corporate or income taxes.

In particular, due to the temporary stagnation in electric vehicle demand (chasm) and the expansion of large-scale upfront investments, core parts and materials companies such as secondary batteries, batteries, and solar power are currently recording massive deficits or experiencing a sharp decline in operating profits. These companies, which have no or negligible corporate taxes to pay, cannot immediately cash in even if they increase domestic production and accumulate tax credit mileage, making it difficult to utilize them as practical investment resources.

Ultimately, a contradiction arises where only a few large conglomerates (Samsung Electronics, SK hynix, Hyundai Motor, Kia, etc.) that are generating solid surpluses and paying large-scale corporate taxes will receive immediate benefits, while battery and parts partner companies that urgently need funding lifelines must carry over the benefits to the distant future.

However, the reason financial authorities such as the Ministry of Economy and Finance are cautious about introducing the direct pay system is interpreted to be because the burden of cash expenditure is enormous amid a severe tax revenue shortfall. Equity issues with existing systems such as R&D or facility investment tax credits, and the potential infringement of the National Assembly’s deliberation rights caused by operating the tax system like a subsidy, are also acting as stumbling blocks.

Experts suggest that for the Korean IRA to become a true savior of the domestic manufacturing ecosystem, it must go beyond a superficial tax benefit and create an unprecedented fund circulation loop.

Specifically, for advanced national strategic technologies such as semiconductors, batteries, and clean hydrogen, which require massive initial investment costs and face fierce global competition, they argue that a direct pay system or a third-party transfer clause that immediately returns the credit amount in cash regardless of surplus or deficit should be introduced in special parallel, even if only temporarily for a minimum of 3 to 5 years.

In addition, a differentiation policy that sets higher credit unit prices for core value chain items is required so that not only large finished vehicle or comprehensive semiconductor companies but also small and medium-sized parts partner companies that support the lower end of the ecosystem can grow together.

If immediate cash support is difficult for the government due to the tax revenue burden, it should promptly prepare indirect supplementary measures, such as first confirming the scale of the credit amount based on production performance, and then allowing the accumulated credit amount to be utilized as collateral for low-interest loans from state-run banks within 1 to 2 years, or supplying liquidity by linking it with government funds.

Impact on the Overall South Korean Economy and Industry

The government’s Korean IRA card is observed to bring about significant shockwaves across the domestic economy, acting as a double-edged sword.

If taxes are reduced in proportion to domestic production volume, the attention of large domestic companies that were contemplating expanding overseas factories will turn back to the domestic market. Investments such as Hyundai Motor’s dedicated electric vehicle factory in Ulsan and the mother factories (core domestic production bases) of the 3 battery companies could gain further momentum. If manufacturing production bases remain domestically, the operation rates of thousands of small and medium-sized materials, parts, and equipment partner companies linked to finished vehicle and semiconductor factories will rise, which leads to a virtuous cycle effect of revitalizing the regional economy and maintaining high-quality manufacturing jobs. Amid external geopolitical crises, it can serve as a cornerstone for strengthening economic security by increasing the self-sufficiency rate of core advanced technologies.

However, such a tax reduction policy will impose an additional tax reduction burden on the already unstable national finances. If only the effect of tax benefits centered on large conglomerates stands out and the trickle-down effect to small and medium-sized parts companies is minimal, the social cost of deepening polarization between large and small and medium-sized enterprises must be paid. Furthermore, there is also a skeptical view on whether the formidable unit price pressure from China-related industries, which are carrying out omnidirectional financial support from the government and indiscriminate low-price offensives, can be defended with only a tax credit at the level of a few %.

Ultimately, the success or failure of the Korean IRA depends on the meticulous selection of targets encompassing the entire supply chain and whether the monetization mechanism, which allows even deficit-ridden companies to immediately feel the benefits, is supplemented. It should not stop at the level of merely sending a signal that ‘we also have a domestic production support system’, and it must be accompanied by a bold and effective tax law amendment so that companies can be certain that running domestic factory lines instead of overseas ones is actually profitable.

text:
In a forceful move against what he describes as entrenched waste, bias, and politicized science in the energy sector, President Donald Trump has ordered a comprehensive review, suspension, and potential debarment of officials tied to fraudulent climate research and manuals used to justify massive regulatory and litigation costs against American energy producers and taxpayers.

The directive, highlighted in a July 20, 2026, post amplifying the President’s statement, targets the National Academy of Sciences (NAS) and related processes that produced biased “climate manuals” for federal judges. These materials have been criticized as one-sided advocacy tools that fueled lawsuits and regulations imposing “massive losses” on the country.

The False Research: Biased Climate Chapter in Judicial Reference Manual

The controversy centers on the Reference Manual on Scientific Evidence, Fourth Edition (published late 2025), a joint project of the Federal Judicial Center (FJC) and the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (NASEM). For the first time, it included a dedicated “Reference Guide on Climate Science” chapter.

Critics, including Republican state attorneys general and outlets like the Wall Street Journal, argued the chapter was biased, written by authors affiliated with climate litigation groups (such as the Sabin Center for Climate Change Law at Columbia University), and designed to influence judges in cases involving fossil fuel companies, attribution of weather events to climate change, and regulatory challenges.

Under pressure, the FJC removed the climate chapter from its version of the manual. However, NASEM kept it available on its website, prompting further backlash. Trump’s statement calls these materials “fraudulent, biased climate manuals” that are “now TOTALLY DISCREDITED,” insisting federal judges deserve “FACTS, not political fraud and fake science.” He ordered a full review, suspension, and debarment of involved officials, declaring taxpayers will no longer fund the “Climate Scam” and judges should never rely on it again.

This fits into broader Trump administration efforts, including the May 2025 Executive Order on Restoring Gold Standard Science, which emphasizes transparency, reproducibility, rigorous peer review, and acknowledgment of uncertainties in federally funded or used research.

Green Graft: Billions (and Trillions) in Questionable Spending on Wind, Solar, Battery Storage, and Carbon Capture

Trump’s review of false research ties directly into scrutiny of the enormous taxpayer-funded push for renewables and related technologies under prior policies, particularly the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) of 2022 and the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA).

Key spending figures include:In fiscal year 2025 alone, federal energy subsidies and tax expenditures totaled approximately $64.1 billion, with renewables, electric vehicles, and energy efficiency capturing roughly 90% (~$57.9–$58 billion). Fossil fuels received only about $2.6 billion. This single-year renewable support exceeded the cumulative fossil fuel tax expenditures from 1994 through 2025.

Broader estimates for IRA clean energy subsidies (wind, solar, batteries, carbon capture, EVs, etc.) have ballooned far beyond initial projections. Independent analyses put the 10-year cost in the range of $936 billion to nearly $2 trillion, with long-term projections reaching several trillion dollars by 2050.

One analysis estimated the U.S. poured about $1.5 trillion into wind and solar since April 2020 (encompassing subsidies, tax credits, private investment spurred by policy, and related support). Despite this, wind and solar together accounted for only around 17% of U.S. electricity generation in 2025.

Specific programs: IIJA and IRA funneled billions into battery storage manufacturing and deployment, carbon capture and storage (CCS) hubs, direct air capture (DAC), and related demonstration projects. DOE has since terminated multiple awards (e.g., over $3.7 billion in CCS/decarbonization projects and hundreds of millions in battery/manufacturing grants) after reviews found them economically unviable or not advancing national energy needs.

Additional examples of questionable spending include attempts to manage or terminate portions of the $14–20 billion “green bank” grants and various clean energy demonstration awards, some canceled due to inadequate documentation, missed milestones, or political considerations in project locations.

The Trump administration has highlighted these as examples of “Green New Scam” funding rushed through without proper oversight, often benefiting projects that increased system costs, relied on intermittent sources, or depended on foreign supply chains. Policies like the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) phased out or restricted many wind and solar tax credits (effective around mid-2026 for new projects), aiming to end market-distorting subsidies for unreliable energy sources.

Moving Forward: Review, Accountability, and Energy Dominance

President Trump’s order signals a broader reset: prioritizing rigorous, unbiased science in policy and judicial decisions while scrutinizing wasteful spending that propped up intermittent renewables and experimental carbon technologies at enormous taxpayer expense. By ending or reviewing subsidies, terminating non-viable projects, and challenging politicized research, the administration argues it will lower energy costs for Americans, enhance grid reliability, reduce dependence on foreign-controlled supply chains, and restore integrity to federal decision-making.

Supporters view this as long-overdue accountability for policies that delivered limited, reliable energy gains relative to the trillions committed or at risk. Critics, including environmental groups and some courts, have challenged certain cancellations and policy shifts, leading to ongoing litigation.

text:
(Berlin) July 20, 2026 – In Europe’s largest automotive market, battery electric cars became about 18 percent cheaper in real terms between 2020 and 2025, even as average prices appeared to rise as a result of a changing model mix. Meanwhile, the number of electric models available on the market has more than quadrupled.

That is the finding of a new joint study by the International Council on Clean Transportation (ICCT) and the Fraunhofer Institute for Systems and Innovation Research ISI, covering the German market as a key indicator of broader European trends. The study draws on more than 100,000 individual data points across six vehicle segments, from small to luxury cars.

“Our results show that the market for electric cars has evolved significantly in recent years. Today, these vehicles offer, on average, longer ranges and more engine power, while the actual prices of comparable models have fallen. This a clear indicator of where Europe’s automotive market is headed,” said Peter Mock, Europe Managing Director at the ICCT.

Average prices rise due to a changing vehicle mix, models themselves are becoming more affordable

In Germany, the average list price for electric vehicles rose nominally from around €37,000 to about €53,000 between 2020 and 2025. However, this increase does not reflect higher prices for comparable vehicles, but rather a shift in the model lineup: The share of mid-range and upper-mid-range vehicles in the electric vehicle lineup rose significantly from 2020 to 2025 and now accounts for 73% of all electric models.

When individual models are tracked over time and vehicle characteristics such as weight, engine power, and range—as well as inflation—are taken into account, the prices of comparable electric vehicles fell by around 18% over the same period. Real prices for vehicles with internal combustion engines, on the other hand, rose by around 2% over the same period.

Battery prices have fallen—savings not yet fully passed on

Global battery prices fell by 21%–24% in nominal terms between 2020 and 2025—from around €165–€185 per kilowatt-hour to about €130–€140. Adjusted for inflation, this corresponds to a price reduction of about 35%–37%. So far, the lower battery prices have had only a limited impact on vehicle prices. However, the average electric range increased by about one-third during the study period, suggesting that savings were invested in vehicle improvements or on recouping research and development costs.

“The significant drop in battery costs has not yet fully translated into lower list prices. This means that the potential for further price reductions in electric vehicles has not yet been exhausted,” explained Prof. Dr. Patrick Plötz, Head of the Department of Energy Technology and Energy Systems at Fraunhofer ISI and one of the study’s authors.

text:
There are several ways the Victorian Government provides incentives and support mechanisms for investing in bioenergy production as part of the state's transition to a circular economy. These include direct grant programs, market-based certificate schemes and federal investment vehicles.

The Department of Energy, Environment and Climate Action (DEECA) manage funds targeted at bioenergy infrastructure, including the $10 million Energy Innovation Fund and the $4 million Victorian Circular Economy Recycling Modernisation Fund.

Biogas projects can generate tradable certificates that provide ongoing revenue streams or offset capital costs through the Victorian Energy Upgrades (VEU) Program, the Australian Carbon Credit Unit (ACCU) Scheme and the Renewable Energy Target’s Large-scale Generation Certificates (LGCs).

Invest Victoria facilitates connections to major federal investment bodies for bioenergy projects, such as the Clean Energy Finance Corporation, the Australian Renewable Energy Agency (ARENA) and the National Reconstruction Fund (NRF).

The Victorian Recycling Infrastructure Plan guides long-term investment and identifies infrastructure gaps to encourage new biogas developments while Landfill Levy Incentives serve as an indirect economic incentive by improving the business case for diverting organic waste to biogas facilities instead of disposal.

A competitive global destination for bioenergy investment, Victoria leads Australian states in committed capital investment for new renewable assets, with over $9.6 billion in the pipeline.

Victoria’s economy is forecast to lead all Australian states in growth from 2026 to 2030 providing a stable environment compared to other global markets. Australia ranks third globally for average green industrial electricity costs, performing better than major regions like Japan, Eastern Europe and most of Asia.

As Australia’s largest food and fibre producer, Victoria has a massive theoretical biogas potential of 80.6 PJ per year, enough to meet 37% of the state's current gas consumption. The Victorian Government’s target to halve organic waste to landfill by 2030 creates a guaranteed demand for biomethane and waste-to-energy projects, while its infrastructure supports significant export potential to the Southeast Asian market.

That leadership, he said, is visible across several fronts — such as its strength in electric vehicles, renewable energy and batteries, sectors that have become central to the global low-carbon transition.

"The 'new three' industries are where China has had a lot of success and where the investment is," Kazaglis said. "It is leading globally, and these are critical areas of the transition."

The comments come as more Chinese companies are playing an increasingly important role in setting science-based climate targets, which require companies to align their emissions-reduction plans with pathways consistent with climate science.

text:
Through this REZ, the Minns Labor Government is leveraging the unique characteristics of the Illawarra region to deliver more affordable and reliable power to NSW homes and businesses, keeping the lights on and downward pressure on power bills.

The Community Reference Group will consist of around 10 member which represent communities in the REZ and help shape the region’s energy future. It will inform how the REZ can support local households, industries and future energy needs and ensure community perspectives are reflected throughout planning.

EnergyCo is seeking a range of volunteers who live locally, including individuals or representatives with relevant experience and expertise from the following groups or backgrounds:

First Nations

Environment

Community

Local government

Education and training

Land use and strategic planning

Social justice

Business and industry

The Illawarra REZ is critical to the state’s energy transition as it has local expertise gained over more than a century of powering Australia.

The Minns Labor Government is shaping this REZ to integrate consumer energy resources such as rooftop solar systems, home batteries and community-scale batteries. Spare government land and commercial roof space is being investigated to minimise impacts on surrounding communities and the environment.

The Community Reference Group builds on insights gained from industry roundtables where experts discussed the local context and the significant opportunities for new industries to develop. These include battery manufacturing, clean energy supply chains and advanced manufacturing, drawing on a workforce with generations of heavy-industry experience.

As work continues to shape Australia’s first urban Renewable Energy Zone, Adam Zarth has been appointed Independent Chair of the Community Reference Group, and David Petrie has been appointed Deputy Independent Chair.

Expressions of Interest close at 5pm on 10 August.

For information, visit www.energyco.nsw.gov.au/our-projects/illawarra-rez.

Minister for the Illawarra and South Coast, Ryan Park said:

“The Illawarra is in a unique position to support the state’s energy transformation and set us up for success as the region’s energy needs grow. We also have the skills and community know-how.

“I encourage locals with experience across community, industry, environment, education, planning and First Nations perspectives to put their hand up and help shape this important work.”

Minister for Planning and Public Spaces, Paul Scully said:

“The Illawarra Urban Renewable Energy Zone is a unique opportunity for our region to help lead the next chapter in clean energy, industry and jobs.

“This Community Reference Group will give locals a direct say in how the Illawarra REZ proceeds, so it reflects the needs of households, workers, businesses and communities.”

EnergyCo Chief Executive Officer, Hannah McCaughey said:

“Tapping local perspectives is essential during the planning stages. A space to discuss community priorities, ideas, and opportunities will inform our approach and ensure the Illawarra community benefits from the REZ.

“These contributions by the Community Reference Group will help us plan the REZ so it delivers for communities and secures our energy grid.”

About the Illawarra Renewable Energy Zone:

EnergyCo is delivering Australia’s first urban REZ in the Illawarra.

The intended network capacity for the Illawarra REZ is 1 gigawatt. This may increase over time with the growth of emerging industries.

The Illawarra REZ will underpin the growth of new low-carbon industries that could service both domestic and export markets as the world decarbonises and shifts towards green manufacturing.

text:
BMW‘s electric M3 is gradually stepping out of the shadows. The naming question is already settled, with M boss Frank van Meel confirming at Goodwood that the car drops the i prefix and simply carries the M3 badge. Now fresh spy shots from the Nürburgring show the high-performance EV wearing less camouflage than before, giving a clearer look at the production model BMW hopes will convince enthusiasts that an M car doesn’t need exhausts to be exhilarating.

Also: BMW’s New Gas M3 Loses Its Grille But Keeps Its Six, And Maybe The Clutch Too

The latest prototype appears heavily influenced by the recently revealed M Concept Neue Klasse, which BMW showcased at Le Mans as a preview of its future electric performance models. While there’s still some disguise covering key details, the overall shape and many of the styling cues now look very close to what buyers can expect when the car finally reaches showrooms.

SH Proshots

Compared to a regular i3 sedan, this prototype looks considerably more aggressive. The swollen wheel arches remain one of the most obvious giveaways, while the car also appears to feature a wider track, rear diffuser and trunk lid spoiler, and a hood vent that wasn’t visible on previous prototypes, but did appear on the concept.

Under the skin, BMW is expected to fit a quad-motor powertrain with one electric motor driving each wheel. While the company hasn’t confirmed output figures, reports continue to suggest the electric M3 could produce more than 700 hp (710 PS), with up to 1,000 hp (1,014 PS) possible on hardcore models later.

The real challenge, however, isn’t straight-line speed. Plenty of EVs can deliver shocking acceleration. What BMW’s engineers need to prove is that this car can deliver the balance, precision and adjustability that have defined generations of M3s. That’s where the four-motor setup could become a genuine advantage, allowing far more precise torque distribution than a conventional all-wheel-drive system.

More Power Than Its Combustion M3 Brother

Fortunately for traditionalists, the electric model won’t replace the combustion-powered M3. BMW is expected to offer both cars simultaneously, with the gasoline version continuing to fly the flag for six-cylinder performance while the EV pushes the brand into new territory. It’s unlikely that the visually similar petrol M3 will make anywhere near as much power as the electric one, though.

SH Proshots

With camouflage steadily disappearing and testing activity ramping up, it looks increasingly likely that we’ll see the finished product sooner rather than later. Whether diehard M fans embrace it is another matter entirely.

title: ASEAN can capture the EU's “carbon tariff” jobs | Lowy Institute
description:
The European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (EU CBAM (Opens in new window)) is reshaping global trade.
Debate over the EU CBAM has largely centred on its effects on trade and climate policy.
Yet one question has received far less attention: what does the EU CBAM mean for jobs?
While the EU CBAM could put some jobs at risk, it could also create new employment opportunities.
Many lack the financial resources and technical expertise needed to measure and report the carbon emissions embedded in their products.
text:
The European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (EU CBAM (Opens in new window)) is reshaping global trade. Often described as a “carbon tariff (Opens in new window)”, the mechanism aims to prevent companies from relocating carbon-intensive production outside Europe to avoid paying for emissions under the EU’s carbon pricing system. Since January 2026, importers of products such as steel, aluminium, cement, fertilisers and hydrogen are required to pay a carbon price on imports from countries that do not have an equivalent carbon pricing regime.

Debate over the EU CBAM has largely centred on its effects on trade and climate policy. Critics and supporters alike have questioned whether it will undermine the competitiveness of exporting countries (Opens in new window), reduce global emissions effectively (Opens in new window), reshape global supply chains (Opens in new window), or accelerate the formation of carbon clubs (Opens in new window).

Yet one question has received far less attention: what does the EU CBAM mean for jobs?

This matters especially in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), a region of more than 350 million workers whose economies are competitive and deeply embedded in global manufacturing and supply chains.

The answer is not straightforward. While the EU CBAM could put some jobs at risk, it could also create new employment opportunities. Ultimately, its impact on employment will depend on how effectively ASEAN economies manage the transition.

The mechanism will not have a uniform impact across ASEAN: exposure varies by export profile and the carbon intensity of individual industries.

Malaysia, Indonesia and Vietnam, for example, are among ASEAN’s largest exporters of iron, steel and aluminium to the EU, sectors covered by the EU CBAM. If firms cannot reduce their emissions or comply with the EU’s reporting requirements, their products may become less competitive in the European market. Companies could lose market share, cut production or divert exports elsewhere, with potential consequences for employment in affected industries.

Compliance itself will also impose costs. Measuring embedded emissions, preparing reports and upgrading production processes require additional investment. Firms may absorb these costs through lower profit margins, pass them on to customers or improve efficiency to remain competitive. For many businesses, particularly those operating on thin margins, these adjustments will not be easy.

The consequences extend well beyond the industries directly covered by the EU CBAM. Steel mills and aluminium producers support extensive networks of transport companies, logistics providers, engineering firms, equipment suppliers and maintenance contractors. If production slows, demand across these linked industries may also be affected

Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) may be particularly vulnerable. Many lack the financial resources and technical expertise needed to measure and report the carbon emissions embedded in their products. New compliance requirements risk widening the gap between large multinational firms – generally those with greater capacity to adapt – and smaller local companies.

Yet focusing only on the risks tells only part of the story. Industrial transitions have always changed the types of jobs economies require, and the transition towards low-carbon production is no exception. Companies will need engineers specialising in renewable energy, industrial electrification and energy-efficient manufacturing, alongside experts in carbon accounting, emissions monitoring, environmental auditing and sustainable supply-chain management.

The transition could also strengthen ASEAN’s competitiveness. Multinational companies are now weighing carbon intensity alongside labour costs when deciding where to invest. Countries that develop cleaner energy systems and low-carbon manufacturing capabilities are likely to become more attractive destinations for investment.

ASEAN is well positioned to benefit from this shift. The region has abundant renewable energy resources, expanding manufacturing capacity and a relatively young workforce. If governments invest in clean infrastructure, workforce development and industrial upgrading, ASEAN could reinforce its position as a global manufacturing hub rather than lose competitiveness.

Encouragingly, several ASEAN countries have already begun preparing for this transition. Singapore (Opens in new window) has introduced a carbon tax, while Indonesia (Opens in new window) and Vietnam (Opens in new window) are developing emissions trading systems. Malaysia (Opens in new window) and Thailand (Opens in new window) are expanding their carbon market initiatives. Although these policies are primarily driven by domestic priorities, the EU CBAM strengthens the economic case for accelerating them. Carbon governance is becoming a source of international competitiveness.

The challenge for ASEAN is not whether the EU CBAM is fair, but whether its workforce is prepared for a changing global economy. Governments should invest in reskilling workers, particularly those employed in carbon-intensive industries. Universities and technical institutions should expand training in renewable energy, industrial efficiency, carbon accounting and digital manufacturing. Businesses, especially SMEs, will also require financial and technical support to adopt cleaner technologies and strengthen emissions reporting.

ASEAN itself has work to do. Rather than responding through fragmented national policies, member states should strengthen regional cooperation on green industrial development and workforce transformation. This could include harmonising carbon accounting standards, developing regional certification and skills-recognition frameworks for green jobs, promoting knowledge-sharing on EU CBAM compliance, and expanding regional financing for industrial decarbonisation. By coordinating their response, ASEAN can reduce adjustment costs, improve the competitiveness of regional supply chains, and position itself as a preferred destination for sustainable investment.

The EU has obligations here, too. If the mechanism is genuinely intended to advance global climate action rather than simply protect European industry, it should be accompanied by greater technical assistance, technology transfer and capacity-building for developing countries. Helping ASEAN industries decarbonise would make the mechanism more effective while reducing concerns that it is merely another form of trade protection.

title: US economy cannot grow without renewables - The Korea Times
description:
But, for decades, American policymakers have also used various policies to fuel household consumption.
Crucially, and more overlooked, is how the US government props up household consumption with energy policy.
With the US holding vast hydrocarbon reserves, this encourages production to exceed demand, leading to systematic underpricing of fossil fuels.
In 2024, wind and solar were, respectively, 53 percent and 41 percent cheaper than fossil fuels.
The American consumer economy can no longer run on fossil fuels.
text:
CHARLOTTESVILLE, VIRGINIA — After the 9/11 terrorist attacks, US President George W. Bush called on Americans to go shopping. While some people claimed at the time that Bush was encouraging irresponsible spending (a criticism that gained traction following the 2008 global financial crisis), he was acknowledging the reality that consumption has long powered America’s formidable economy.

Over the past 20 years, household consumption has, on average, accounted for roughly 56 percent of the United States’ annual GDP growth — reflecting an atypical economic structure that is both an unintended byproduct of dollar dominance and the result of a deliberate growth strategy.

The dollar’s position as the world’s reserve currency has inadvertently created ideal conditions for the profligate U.S. consumer. Providing dollars to the rest of the world enables the U.S. to run current-account deficits indefinitely. Moreover, high demand for dollar-denominated assets pushes up the greenback’s exchange rate, making U.S. exports relatively more expensive, boosting imports, and contributing to the decline of U.S. manufacturing.

But, for decades, American policymakers have also used various policies to fuel household consumption. In housing, for example, the U.S. government has long offered mortgage-debt relief, tax credits, and subsidies, allowing homeowners to use their property as collateral to borrow more. Similar, the government derisks lending for the financial sector through loan backstops and liquidity, which creates a kind of “finance culture” that normalizes spending beyond one’s means.

Crucially, and more overlooked, is how the US government props up household consumption with energy policy. High energy consumption is central to the American way of life. Houses are larger, requiring more energy to construct, heat, and cool. Compared to much of the rest of the world, Americans purchase more (and larger) cars, drive for longer distances, and consume more meat and other carbon-intensive goods.

Moreover, the U.S. government has subsidized the oil and gas industry for more than a century through the tax code’s treatment of intangible drilling costs. With the US holding vast hydrocarbon reserves, this encourages production to exceed demand, leading to systematic underpricing of fossil fuels.

But the energy landscape is changing, owing to soaring energy prices for US households and the plummeting costs of renewables. The problem is that US President Donald Trump, while recognizing that abundant, cheap energy underpins America’s consumption-led growth model, conflates that with fossil fuels, confusing historic correlation with causation.

Trump’s “drill, baby, drill” agenda has sought to boost oil and gas production, even as other countries phase out fossil fuels. His administration’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) has increased subsidies for the oil and gas industry while repealing nearly all of the tax credits enacted by the Biden administration’s Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) to accelerate the uptake of clean energy.

Research from Princeton University’s ZERO Lab projected that, by 2030, the OBBBA would raise US household and business energy costs by $28 billion. One year after the bill’s passage, that prediction seems to be coming to fruition and may even end up being optimistic, as supply shocks from the Iran war and the AI data-center boom cause energy prices to surge. Last year, data centers accounted for around half of new US electricity demand, with rapid growth potentially causing consumers’ electricity bills to increase by as much as 25% in some regions by 2030.

Meanwhile, the price of renewable energy continues to fall to new lows. In 2024, wind and solar were, respectively, 53 percent and 41 percent cheaper than fossil fuels. The months-long closure of the Strait of Hormuz, which severely disrupted global oil and gas flows, has led countries around the world to embrace renewables, using green technologies largely manufactured by China. Even in the U.S., consumer demand for electric vehicles has spiked along with inflation.

The American consumer economy can no longer run on fossil fuels. To maintain growth, the US must follow the lead of other countries and scale up renewables. Reviving the IRA, which was primarily focused on energy abundance, is an obvious first step.

To be sure, many policymakers in the U.S. and the European Union are concerned that Chinese green tech poses security risks; the EU has even moved to ban inverters from China. But the best way to address these anxieties is by modernizing existing manufacturing to produce high-risk components like inverters domestically, while continuing to import secure, low-cost parts, like the solar panels themselves. This would require implementing industrial policy, but nothing outside the norm.

The Trump administration’s grim determination to ignore clean energy is not only costly; it also jeopardizes long-term economic growth. Actively suppressing renewables as fossil-fuel prices steadily rise will be the death knell for a growth model built on the promise of cheap energy.

Daniel Driscoll, Assistant Professor of Sociology at the University of Virginia and a nonresident fellow at the Roosevelt Institute, is the author of the forthcoming Why Carbon Taxes Failed (Oxford University Press, August 2026). This article was distributed by Project Syndicate.

description:

text:
A China-focused model maps how tightening lithium, cobalt, and nickel supplies could reshape the pace, cost, and carbon benefits of vehicle electrification.

Paper: Reshaping vehicle electrification pathways under the metal-carbon trade-off. Image credit: AI-generated image created using ChatGPT/OpenAI

The rapid adoption of electric vehicles (EVs) is crucial for reducing transport-related carbon emissions; however, their long-term success depends partly on the availability of critical battery materials. A recent 'article in press' in the journal Communications Earth & Environment examined how constraints in the supply of lithium, cobalt, and nickel influence future EV adoption and emissions. Using the Collaborative Optimization Model for Carbon Emission Reduction and Metal Resource Security (COMERS), researchers estimated that ignoring these constraints could overestimate China's passenger EV ownership by as much as 42% in 2060 while underestimating cumulative passenger-car carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions and transition costs.

The findings highlight the necessity of incorporating material availability into long-term transport and climate planning to produce realistic decarbonization pathways.

The Demand-Supply Challenge of Critical Metals

The transition to low-carbon transportation relies on the widespread adoption of battery electric vehicles (BEVs) and plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs). These vehicles depend heavily on lithium-ion batteries, whose high-energy-density cathodes require critical metals such as cobalt (Co), lithium (Li), and nickel (Ni). As countries strive to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050, the International Energy Agency projects that demand for these minerals could increase by 19 to 42 times by 2040 as compared with 2020.

Meeting this demand poses a significant challenge, as these minerals are finite and unevenly distributed, with most reserves concentrated in a few countries. This geographic concentration increases the risk of supply shortages, price volatility, and supply-chain disruptions as demand grows. As a result, the availability of critical battery materials has become an important factor in determining the pace and cost of vehicle electrification.

Bridging Vehicle Electrification and Power Generation

To investigate this material-carbon dilemma, researchers developed the COMERS model, which relates the passenger vehicle sector to the power generation system. This model captures feedback between EV deployment, vehicle retirement, recycling, electricity demand, and mineral availability. It combines multi-sector cost optimization with dynamic material flow analysis to track the life cycle of critical metals, from primary supply and battery production to vehicle use, retirement, recycling, and secondary material recovery. Vehicle ownership is projected using a Gompertz model, while long-term mineral supply is estimated with a Hubbert model.

Researchers evaluated seven scenarios representing different pathways, including variations in recycling efficiency, mineral supply constraints, international trade conditions, and battery chemistries, such as low-cobalt and cobalt-free cathodes. A separate non-metal-constraint scenario (NMS) without mineral supply limitations was also included to isolate the effects of resource scarcity on EV adoption, carbon emissions, and transition costs. Furthermore, the framework was applied to China, the world's largest EV market, where external dependence on these metals ranges from 72% to 97%.

Implications of Ignoring Mineral Constraints

The optimization results showed that ignoring critical mineral constraints leads to overly optimistic projections for transport decarbonization. Compared with the six material-constrained scenarios, the unconstrained NMS scenario overestimated EV deployment while underestimating cumulative carbon dioxide emissions by up to 57%, equivalent to 6.1 billion tonnes, and passenger-car transition costs by up to 6%, equivalent to 16.9 trillion renminbi (RMB), at constant 2023 prices between 2025 and 2060. It predicted an earlier automotive carbon peak in 2027, whereas incorporating mineral constraints delayed the peak to 2030-2034 as slower EV adoption extends the use of internal combustion engine vehicles.

The analysis identified a scenario-dependent sequential supply bottleneck for battery materials: lithium is the primary constraint before 2035, while declining cobalt production becomes the dominant limiting factor thereafter in the REF, FRS, HCS, and LCS scenarios. Under the low-cobalt and cobalt-free scenarios, lithium remained the sole modeled bottleneck until approximately 2046. Across the modeled scenarios, cumulative demand for lithium and cobalt across all end uses in China could exceed China's 2023 reserves by factors of 2.2-3.1 and 49-86, respectively. Although lithium supply is projected to continue growing through 2060, global primary nickel and cobalt production are expected to peak around 2035 and 2045 before declining.

Recommendations for Sustainable Battery Development

The results provide practical guidance for battery development and resource planning. Reducing cobalt dependence through low-cobalt chemistries, such as NMC811, and cobalt-free lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries can ease pressure on cobalt supplies while lowering modeled cumulative CO2 emissions by 1.4-1.7 billion tonnes. However, under the ETS scenario in 2060, NMC811 increased demand for lithium and nickel, while LFP continued to require lithium, showing that chemistry changes redistribute rather than eliminate mineral pressures. The authors emphasize the importance of developing lower-cobalt battery technologies to improve the resilience of EV supply chains.

The analysis also highlights the role of a circular battery economy. In an idealized full-recycling scenario in which collection of batteries and other end-of-life products reaches 100% by 2060, secondary materials could supply up to 69% of lithium, 79% of cobalt, and 88% of nickel demand in that year. The authors recommend establishing strategic mineral reserves, prioritizing immediate lithium reserves and cobalt reserves before 2035, to help buffer against supply disruptions and price volatility. Together, these measures could help provide a secure material foundation for large-scale vehicle electrification.

Planning for a Low-Carbon Transportation Future

In summary, the COMERS model demonstrates that achieving low-carbon transport requires coordinated planning across the vehicle, material, and power sectors. The analysis shows that incorporating critical mineral constraints into the strategy yields more realistic projections of EV adoption, emissions, and transition costs than models that assume unlimited material availability. While improvements in battery chemistry and recycling can reduce resource pressure, they are insufficient to achieve net-zero transport without a carbon-neutral or negative-emissions power system or the removal of residual emissions through carbon sinks.

The framework provides practical guidance for policymakers and industry leaders seeking to align mineral supply, battery manufacturing, vehicle deployment, and power-system expansion. Because COMERS was applied empirically only to China, its relevance to Germany, Japan, Korea, and other manufacturing economies is inferred rather than directly modeled. Incorporating material constraints into long-term planning could nevertheless help reduce investment risks and strengthen supply-chain resilience.

However, the projections are conditional on assumptions about future mineral production, battery-market shares, vehicle use, recycling, and China's electricity emission factor declining to zero by 2060. The model also excludes sodium-ion batteries, hydrogen vehicles, and potential constraints involving aluminum, copper, and steel, and its emissions estimates do not represent a complete cradle-to-grave assessment.

name: EPA
title: NJDEP budget cuts are part of the war on the environment - The Jersey Vindicator
description:
The New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection budget has been signed, and it reveals exactly where the state’s priorities lie.
The DEP budget used to represent a commitment to protecting our air, water, parks, wildlife, and public health.
The state budget cuts the department’s direct state appropriation by $150 million, dropping it from $662 million to $512 million.
The Clean Energy Fund has become Trenton’s favorite ATM For the 18th consecutive year, New Jersey has raided the Clean Energy Fund.
Phil Murphy continued cutting the DEP budget and staff while failing to fully restore staffing or strengthen many of the protections weakened under Christie.
text:
Permit giveaways, budget raids, and weakened enforcement are reshaping New Jersey’s environmental agency.

The New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection budget has been signed, and it reveals exactly where the state’s priorities lie. A budget is a roadmap. It shows what the government values and what it is willing to invest in. The DEP budget used to represent a commitment to protecting our air, water, parks, wildlife, and public health. Today, it is being transformed into something very different: the Department of Expedited Permits.

The Sherrill administration talks about “efficiency,” “cutting red tape,” and “modernizing government.” Don’t be fooled. When politicians say they’re cutting red tape, what they usually mean is they’re cutting environmental protections. They’re replacing science with stopwatches, public participation with corporate consultations, and environmental review with rubber stamps.

This isn’t simply about making permits move faster. It is about changing the mission of the DEP itself. Instead of asking whether projects should be approved or how their impacts can be minimized, the focus is now on how quickly permits can be issued. They have even renamed permit applicants as “customers.”

The result is a dangerous combination of budget cuts, weakened enforcement, fast-track permitting, climate rollbacks, and billions of dollars in subsidies for dirty and risky energy projects. It is an agenda that puts corporate developers, fossil fuel companies, and politically connected industries ahead of the people of New Jersey.

This isn’t environmental policy. It’s the continuation of the war on environmental protection.

Starving the DEP while expecting the public not to notice

You cannot protect the environment while cutting the very agency responsible for protecting it.

The DEP is facing one of its largest financial cutbacks in years. The state budget cuts the department’s direct state appropriation by $150 million, dropping it from $662 million to $512 million. Including federal reductions, DEP funding has fallen by nearly $253 million, including an $84.3 million loss in federal funding, an 11.5% overall reduction.

At the very moment New Jersey faces stronger storms, worsening flooding, sea levels rising, PFAS contamination, wildfire threats, drinking water problems, and aging infrastructure, Trenton has decided the DEP should do more with substantially less. Apparently, someone in the State House believes climate change takes budget cuts into consideration, especially after the Climate Superfund bill was killed.

Instead of strengthening environmental protection, lawmakers eliminated $8 million for Green Acres Urban Parks grants, cut $6.6 million from water infrastructure programs, and slashed funding for the Council on Green Jobs by 50%, while adding $4.3 million to fast-track permitting.

These aren’t just numbers on a spreadsheet. They mean fewer parks in urban communities, delayed replacement of aging water systems, fewer opportunities to train workers for clean energy jobs, and fewer investments in healthier neighborhoods.

The annual budget shell game

Every year, lawmakers propose eliminating $1.3 million for the New Jersey School of Conservation and its outstanding environmental education program for schoolchildren. Every year, there is a public outcry, advocates spend weeks lobbying to restore the money, and every year it is reinstated.

It’s political theater.

The fight diverts environmental groups from battling the real damage: $150 million in DEP budget cuts, raids on clean energy funds, and policies that fast-track permits while weakening environmental protections.

Meanwhile, lawmakers somehow found new money to speed up permit approvals.

That tells you everything you need to know about their priorities.

They added money to process permits faster but couldn’t find enough money to hire inspectors to ensure permit holders actually obey the law. That’s like hiring more ticket agents at an airport while firing the mechanics who inspect the airplanes.

The message is clear:

Developers get customer service.

The public gets fewer protections and less accountability.

The Clean Energy Fund has become Trenton’s favorite ATM

For the 18th consecutive year, New Jersey has raided the Clean Energy Fund. Think about that.

A fund created to reduce pollution, lower energy costs, promote renewable energy, weatherize homes, and fight climate change has become Trenton’s favorite budget-balancing gimmick. This year alone, $140 million is being diverted from the Clean Energy Fund to support NJ Transit.

NJ Transit certainly needs stable funding. But balancing one budget by robbing another isn’t fiscal responsibility. It’s political accounting.

You don’t solve one crisis by creating another.

Even more alarming, the state authorized diversions of up to $510 million from Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative revenues, including transfers into the Clean Energy Fund and the Board of Public Utilities for short-term utility bill credits. These climate programs were never intended to become permanent piggy banks.

RGGI revenue comes from carbon pollution allowances. It was supposed to reduce emissions, improve energy efficiency, expand renewable energy, help communities adapt to climate change, and reduce pollution in overburdened neighborhoods.

Apparently, Trenton’s motto is: Bet you can’t steal just one.

The Clean Energy Fund raid was supposed to last one year. Eighteen years later, they’re still doing it. Once politicians start raiding environmental funds, they rarely stop. That’s what is so scary about taking the RGGI money. It will not stop.

Every diversion delays energy-efficiency projects. Every raid postpones renewable energy investments. Every dollar stolen today means more pollution, higher emissions, and greater costs tomorrow. The irony and hypocrisy couldn’t be greater.

The same politicians who give speeches about climate leadership are quietly draining the very programs designed to fight climate change. It’s like bragging you’re on a diet while eating a hot fudge sundae because you had a Diet Coke with it.

Parks without protection

Our state parks tell the same story.

Years of underfunding have created an estimated $400 million maintenance backlog and $1.5 billion in needed capital repairs and upgrades. Our parks are deteriorating.

In 1993, Parks and Forestry employed 1,200 people. Today, there are only about 600 employees, despite managing 40% more land.

Historic buildings continue to decay, and many have been demolished. Swimming areas close. Bathrooms remain locked. Wildlife Management Areas are understaffed. Some close. Visitor facilities continue to deteriorate. Naturalists and park historians have disappeared through attrition.

Federal cuts also eliminated approximately $31.5 million from the Land and Water Conservation Fund and another $17 million from urban forestry programs.

Meanwhile, the DEP is sitting on approximately $750 million in unspent Green Acres funds and another $400 million for farmland preservation.

Land acquisition has slowed dramatically:

• 1999-2009: 18,000-20,000 acres annually

• 2009-2019: 12,000-13,500 acres annually

• Since 2019: About 5,400 acres annually

Forests are one of New Jersey’s best defenses against climate change. They store carbon, reduce ambient temperatures, protect drinking water, reduce flooding, recharge aquifers, prevent erosion, and provide critical wildlife habitat. Yet they receive less attention while politicians rush to subsidize energy projects and speed development approvals.

Apparently, paving over open space has become easier than protecting it.

Enforcement is being replaced by expediency

Perhaps the greatest irony is that while politicians insist permits must move faster, they continue weakening the very enforcement programs that ensure environmental laws are followed.

Enforcement has been downgraded from an independent division to an office under the commissioner. Enforcement staff has declined by 40%, while the DEP hired 50 new employees to accelerate permit approvals.

Meanwhile, EMR in Camden keeps catching fire. The Pioneers Metal Finishing Superfund site caught fire. Galaxie Chemical in Paterson caught fire.

Permits are only meaningful if someone verifies compliance. There are now so few enforcement staff that they often respond only to emergencies. Many violations of environmental laws simply go unenforced. Without inspectors, monitoring, and enforcement, permits become little more than pieces of paper.

Environmental laws are only as strong as the people enforcing them. They are the cops on the environmental beat. Without them, there will be more accidents, more mistakes, more deliberate destruction of our environment, and more pollution.

New Jersey is moving toward a system where permits are accelerated, inspections are reduced, enforcement is weakened, and polluters face less oversight. That isn’t government efficiency. It’s government surrender.

And when enforcement disappears, pollution gets worse.

A 30-year war on environmental protection

The effort to dismantle the DEP didn’t begin today.

It began in 1994, when Gov. Christine Todd Whitman cut the DEP budget by roughly one-third, laid off about one-third of its staff, rolled back regulations, and weakened enforcement. During her administration, enforcement actions dropped by nearly 80%, and two chemical plants exploded. She also attempted to weaken Clean Water protections, triggering one of New Jersey’s biggest environmental battles.

Public outrage over those cuts led Republican senators, with Democratic support, to dedicate Corporate Business Tax revenues to environmental programs such as watershed protection and contaminated-site cleanup. That momentum also helped secure Whitman’s eventual support for open-space preservation.

Gov. James E. McGreevey restored some funding and staffing. He advanced major environmental protections, including Category One stream buffers and the Highlands Act. Progress continued under Gov. Richard Codey and during the early years of the Corzine administration.

Then the rollback resumed. Gov. Jon Corzine froze hiring, cut the budget, began raiding the Clean Energy Fund, privatized toxic-site cleanups, and got rid of the award-winning independent Division of Science.

Gov. Chris Christie declared open war on environmental protection, cutting the DEP budget by another 25%, laying off staff, using “Red Tape Review” to roll back dozens of environmental rules and standards, and even stopping the legally required enforcement reports to the Legislature.

Gov. Phil Murphy continued cutting the DEP budget and staff while failing to fully restore staffing or strengthen many of the protections weakened under Christie. He got rid of the independent Division of Enforcement.

Now the Sherrill administration is continuing the pattern with more budget cuts, more “red tape” reviews, and faster permitting.

The bottom line

In 1994, the DEP represented 1.2% of the state budget. Today it is only 0.5%. The DEP had approximately 4,300 full-time employees. Today it has about 2,700.

The numbers would be even worse without dedicated Corporate Business Tax funding, which now provides roughly 18% of the DEP budget, increased federal funding at about 48%, and permitting fees.

Ironically, the DEP is one of the few state agencies that largely pays for itself while helping fund programs in other agencies.

At the same time, the department has taken on dozens of new responsibilities, including Environmental Justice, climate programs, PFAS regulation, resilience planning, and managing 40% more public land, all with significantly fewer employees.

The reality is simple. The DEP no longer has enough staff to properly maintain our parks, inspect facilities, enforce environmental laws, prosecute violators, protect our air and water, clean up toxic sites, or respond to the growing threats of climate change.

There may not be enough staff to protect New Jersey’s environment or deal with an environmental emergency. But there will always seem to be enough staff to fast-track and rubber-stamp permits to cut down forests, pave over farmland, fill in wetlands, weaken protections, and accelerate environmental destruction.

text:
The Aspen School District has reported a successful test bore dug into the ground beneath the football field that reached 1,000 feet into the earth, nearly double what the industry norm is and one of the deepest ground source geothermal installations in Colorado history.

The geothermal test bore is a milestone in the district’s $5 million state-funded project to bring a thermal energy network to 400,000 square feet of district facilities. According to a press release, reaching 1,000 feet is a “relatively rare” occurrence in ground source geothermal work — most bores range from 300 to 600 feet.

“Hitting that 1,000 foot test bore hole this week was monumental,” ASD Director of Operations Joe Waneka told The Aspen Times. “The iron is hot. We’re very excited for that.”

Waneka confirmed that a test bore attempt at the end of last year only made it 67 feet. This time, drilling contractor PanTerra Energy made it all the way utilizing two different drilling rigs; for the top 250 feet, a drill that can go through cobble easier was used, taking about four or five days total for this section with starts and stops, and for the additional 750 a different rig was used to go through the solid bedrock, completed in the equivalent of only two days.

To be able to reach 1,000 feet in depth both increases the heat exchange capacity of each well and reduces the total number of bores needed for a project. For this project, Ashley Brasovan, senior account executive at McKinstry, confirmed that while an initial estimation of around 300 bores was expected, the successful test bore could reduce the number of bores drills by up to half, potentially around 150.

“It’s a lot less disruptive overall to campus,” Brasovan said of being able to reduce that number. “You want to limit the number of holes — that limits the amount of risk overall on the project.”

She highlighted that, in addition to saving space, fewer holes will also save cost.

The next step will be a conductivity test of the geo bore, which Waneka called “paramount” to the continued success of the project. Once the pipe is down and grouted, the hole will rest for a week before the thermal conductivity is measured over 48 hours — it will then take two to three weeks to produce a report that will provide the information used to determine the final number of bores that will be drilled.

Once completed, the thermal energy network will provide low-carbon heating and cooling across the Aspen School District campus by connecting the district’s heating, ventilation and air conditioning systems to the ground source heat pumps on a central loop and bore field, according to the release. The project is aiming to stabilize long-term energy costs while significantly reducing fossil fuel use.

“The project arrives at a pivotal moment for Colorado’s geothermal industry,” the release adds. “A project of ASD’s scale would represent a meaningful share of Colorado’s total geothermal drilling in 2027-2028 and is exactly the kind of pipeline necessary to grow the industry.”

According to Peter Baumann, communications manager at Clean Energy Economy for the Region who are partnering with Aspen School District, McKinstry, PanTerra Energy, GreyEdge Group and Holy Cross Energy, the project is a “future, forward-looking” endeavor. Lauren Suhrbier, director of strategic development at Clean Energy Economy for the Region, noted in the press release that a strong project pipeline is “one of the best ways to grow Colorado’s geothermal market.”

She added in the release, “Through its role on the project and participation in the Colorado Geothermal Council’s workforce development group, CLEER is helping translate these lessons from ASD and McKinstry into statewide planning and grant efforts. Most importantly, ASD’s leadership, along with McKinstry’s and PanTerra Energy’s work to deliver the project, illustrates what is possible for Colorado’s growing geothermal industry.”

The project is funded by the $5 million Geothermal Energy Tax Credit Offering award, one of seven awards totaling $12.4 million from the Colorado Energy Office, as well as a $78,400 Geothermal Energy Grant Program award and a $50,000 grant from Aspen Community Office for Resource Efficiency for feasibility work. Additional funding will come from a federal tax credit covering 30% to 40% of eligible project costs, an energy performance contract and a districtwide bond approved by voters in 2025.

“Without the community, this wouldn’t have been viable,” Waneka said. “Without taxpayer vote of confidence … we wouldn’t be doing this.”

Final design will be completed this year, the release confirms, and groundbreaking is expected for 2027 after the school year finishes.

Used EV Market Boom

If you have been holding back from buying an EV, grabbing one on a massive discount from the secondhand market might be a brilliant idea right now. Records show that off-lease EVs are heavily entering the market after their initial leasing plans officially lapse. This sudden, unprecedented surge in supply is causing dealership prices to plummet, making advanced electric mobility highly accessible for budget-conscious drivers everywhere.

Already, the general motoring public is warming up to the idea of getting electric vehicles for a mere fraction of the original showroom cost. As new electric car sales continue to slump globally due to high interest rates, the used EV market actively sets transaction records month after month. However, before you sign on the dotted line for that heavily depreciated bargain, you must truly understand the reality of maintaining them and exactly what components actually break down over time.

It's the Devil You Still Know

According to an insightful study from UK extended car warranty provider Warrantywise, owning an older electric vehicle brings incredibly familiar headaches. By analyzing proprietary repair requests between January 2023 and January 2026, they discovered that common EV faults closely mirror those of traditional internal combustion cars, making the battery the absolute last thing to worry about.

The usual expensive repair suspects arise from basic suspension systems, frustrating electrical niggles, and easily damaged auxiliary sensors. In fact, real-world examples show that original EV batteries easily outlast the vehicle's surrounding hardware, proving their long-term durability. Keep in mind that, since EV volumes remain significantly lower than those of gas cars, this directional data is highly sensitive to model mix and should absolutely not be taken as strict financial advice.

Be Wary When Buying Used

While traditional mechanical and electrical faults heavily dominate repair charts, this rightly reminds everyone that the main power pack should still be thoroughly examined. That certainly doesn't mean battery health isn't important, because when they do eventually fail, they are incredibly expensive. Across Warrantywise repair requests, the average high-voltage battery repair cost was a massive $8,173, underscoring why prospective buyers must still pay close attention to battery condition before purchasing a used EV.

Anthony Diggins, Managing Director, summarized the current maintenance landscape perfectly for hesitant shoppers. "It's still early days for EV repair data, but some interesting trends are starting to emerge. While EV battery failures often receive the most attention, our repair data suggests they're only part of the story," he explained. Diggins noted that a broader range of electrical, charging, and suspension components requires repairs, highlighting the importance of understanding the overall ownership experience rather than focusing on a single component. EVs are apparently still regular cars with moving parts; always properly check used EVs before bringing one home.

text:
Texas is confronting a widening gap between its long-term water supply and the needs of its growing population and economy.

The draft 2027 State Water Plan projects that supplies available during a drought of record will decline from 15.5 million acre-feet annually in 2030 to nearly 14 million by 2080, primarily because of aquifer depletion. Without new supplies or conservation measures, Texas could face shortages of 3.6 million acre-feet in 2030 and 5.8 million by 2080.

Corpus Christi has seen prolonged drought and rising industrial consumption exposed weaknesses in planning based largely on previous droughts. Water-supply projections repeatedly fell as newer droughts proved worse than earlier records.

Artificial-intelligence and cloud-computing data centers create another rapidly expanding demand. A University of Texas study estimates data centers—which use water directly for cooling and indirectly for electricity generation—could account for 3% to 9% of statewide water use by 2040. Researchers caution that the range remains uncertain because cooling technologies and development rates vary.

Texas planners recommend conservation, reuse, desalination, reservoirs and other projects. But implementing the state plan’s proposed projects could cost nearly $174 billion, underscoring the difficult choices ahead.

text:
Hyundai and Rivian are both opting into California's instant rebate of up to $3,500 for people buying their first electric vehicle.

As USA Today detailed, the duo's moves offer a measure of help after federal EV tax credits disappeared.

What's happening?

California's new MyFirstEV program is for residents purchasing their first EV, as the Governor's office described in a statement. Under the plan, eligible new EV buyers could get $3,500 off, while qualifying used EV buyers could receive $1,750.

The money is expected to be available by the end of the summer through a $135 million state budget agreement and grants funded by automakers.

"With our new instant rebate program for electric vehicles, we're making it easier for families to drive clean, breathe clean, and keep more money in their pockets," California Gov. Gavin Newsom said in the statement.

Since participation is voluntary for carmakers, only brands that opt in will be able to offer the rebate. Hyundai told USA Today on July 15 that it intends to join Irvine-based Rivian in the program, which opted in earlier in the week.

In most cases, qualifying new EVs must be priced below $50,000, and used EVs must come in under $25,000. The outlet noted California-based zero-emission vehicle companies are not subject to those price ceilings, which is a setup that could favor domestic companies Rivian and Lucid.

Why does it matter?

The rebate arrives after the federal government ended its popular $7,500 EV tax credit on Sept. 30, 2025. With new EV prices averaging nearly $55,000, California is trying to make the upfront cost of going electric less daunting for households.

EVs can help drivers save money over time on fuel and maintenance while also reducing tailpipe pollution that contributes to unhealthy air. In a state long affected by smog and wildfire-related air quality issues, that can translate into real public health benefits.

California remains the nation's largest EV market. The Alliance for Automotive Innovation said EVs and hybrids made up 17.5% of the state's new light-duty vehicle registrations in early 2026. USA Today reported California was the only state to top a 20% market share in 2025.

The effects may not stop at the state line. California's vehicle standards often influence other governments, and 17 states in recent years have adopted at least part of California's clean car regulations, according to the outlet.

What's being done?

California is stepping in where federal policy has retreated. The state is targeting first-time EV buyers across all income levels rather than limiting the benefit to higher earners.

Officials say more automakers are expected to join the program soon. Lindsay Buckley, a spokeswoman with the California Air Resources Board, wrote the agency expects to announce the full list within the next month in an email to USA Today.
