title: NextEra, Dominion detail reasons, terms of proposed merger - Daily Press
description:
Dominion Energy wasn’t looking for anything like it when NextEra Energy’s feeler about a merger landed out of the blue in November.
“Dominion did not enter into the Merger Agreement lightly,” Blue said.
Firewalls The filing says there would be a firewall around Dominion’s Virginia utility after the merger.
As part of the merger agreement, approved by both companies’ boards, Dominion’s Virginia utility will not assume any debt from any other entity within the merged company.
Dominion Energy Virginia is also expected to receive a one-notch upgrade at S&P, from BBB+ to A-.
text:
Dominion Energy wasn’t looking for anything like it when NextEra Energy’s feeler about a merger landed out of the blue in November.

The utility had a pending rate increase before the State Corporation Commission, and there was the question of the $1.47 billion gas-fired power plant it wanted to build in Chesterfield County and possible legislative changes in the 2026 General Assembly session.

“When NextEra first approached Dominion about this idea in November 2025, the Board of Directors and management of Dominion were not looking for a merger,” Dominion chairman and chief executive officer Bob Blue told the State Corporation Commission, which last week started its review of the $67 billion deal.

“We were executing well then and continue to execute well … This includes our near completion of the Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind Project, our continuing development of the largest solar generation portfolio in the PJM transmission region, our life extension projects for the four baseload nuclear units at the North Anna and Surry Power Stations, our planned addition of new dispatchable generation resources, and many other generation, transmission, and distribution system investments,” Blue said.

But, “with that said, the utility industry is clearly facing historic challenges associated with unprecedented load growth,” especially in a Virginia that’s home to the largest concentration of data centers in the world, he said.

“Against that backdrop, it is clear that there are overarching benefits from greater scale, financial strength and operational breadth and expertise for utility operators such as Dominion and NextEra going forward,” he said.

And so, the two firms decided to talk.

Now, it is up to the State Corporation Commission, along with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission and state regulators in North and South Carolina to decide if the two can go ahead with the merger they agreed on. Stockholders of both firms must also approve.

“Dominion did not enter into the Merger Agreement lightly,” Blue said. “After careful consideration, Dominion concluded that combining with NextEra will enhance the Company’s ability to meet the significant challenges and opportunities ahead.”

NextEra’s commitments

In a filing with the SCC, Dominion and NextEra detailed their financial and operating agreements that make their combination unlike many mergers.

In most cases, the acquiring firm expects gains from layoffs and cutting other costs.

Instead, NextEra shareholders are paying for $1.78 billion in bill credits for Dominion’s Virginia customers, and smaller amounts for Dominion’s North Carolina and South Carolina customers.

On a benchmark 1,000-kilowatt-hour monthly bill, which now costs $180.79, that will total $10 over the two years following completion of the merger.

NextEra is also funding a $10 million increase in Dominion’s charitable giving, as well as a $360 million cash payment to Dominion shareholders, in addition to an exchange of 0.8138 NextEra shares for each Dominion share, a swap analysts value at $67 billion.

“NextEra understands that this transaction should deliver demonstrable value for customers. The bill credit commitment is substantial, and it was not made lightly,” NextEra chairman and chief executive officer John Ketchum told the commission.

“That commitment reflects the importance of customer bills at a time when utilities across the country are facing upward pressure on costs from load growth, infrastructure investment, storm risk, supply chain constraints, and resource needs,” he said.

NextEra, with shares of stock more favored by Wall Street than Dominion’s, has committed to providing the necessary stock and retained earnings financing to maintain Dominion’s investment plans for its system.

It will do so at levels that support Dominion’s credit ratings which as set to rise to a high-grade level.

Critics

Early critics had charged that the merger would change Dominion’s current long-term planning document, which calls for installing about 17,500 megawatts of solar facilities, 3,460 megawatts of wind turbines, 2,000 megawatts of battery storage, 1,944 megawatts from small modular reactors and 8,510 megawatts of gas-fired plants.

They’ve also pointed to the sharp rise in rates that came when Florida regulators approved increases for Gulf Power after NextEra acquired it in 2019, as well as the $7 billion, multiyear increase NextEra’s Florida Power and Light subsidiary won earlier this year — the largest dollar amount ever, which represents a 2% a year increase that sets the Florida utility’s residential rates at 13.9 cents per kilowatt-hour versus Dominion’s 18.1 cents.

“As Virginians, we don’t want to cede decision-making for our largest electric utility to out-of-state corporate interests that won’t live with the consequences of those decisions,” said Peter Anderson, energy policy director for Appalachian Voices.

Firewalls

The filing says there would be a firewall around Dominion’s Virginia utility after the merger.

As part of the merger agreement, approved by both companies’ boards, Dominion’s Virginia utility will not assume any debt from any other entity within the merged company.

The SCC’s strict oversight of utility dealings with affiliate companies would continue to apply.

The two companies agreed that Dominion Energy Virginia will not pledge its assets to support affiliate debt, and would not guarantee affiliate obligations or enter into agreements where it could be at risk from an affiliate firm’s financial distress.

Dominion’s Virginia utility would continue to hold property in its name — formally speaking, the utility’s assets and debt are all in the name of Virginia Electric and Power Company — and would keep its accounting systems, bank accounts and financial records separate.

The utility will not transfer or dispose of any assets, change the territory it services or any of its currently approved rates and terms of service as a result of the merger.

The size and membership of the board of directors of Dominion Energy Virginia will not change, and Blue will remain its chairman while the utility’s president, Ed Baine, will remain in his post. The two firms agreed that the Virginia utility’s president must always be a Virginia resident.

Dominion will retain control of its $11.2 billion offshore wind project, 27 miles in the Atlantic off the Virginia Beach Oceanfront, with its 176 turbines that will generate enough electricity to power up to 660,000 homes.

And, “To be clear, nothing about this Merger will change the Company’s vigilance to ensure that data centers continue to ‘pay their fair share’ of the investments and costs required to serve them, and that those customers are not being subsidized by other customers,” Blue said, citing the company’s new rate class and contract terms designed to keep what it spends to connect data centers from shifting to other ratepayers.

Another big difference from many corporate mergers is a guarantee that Dominion employees’ jobs will be protected for 18 months with two-year compensation and benefits protection for non-union employees. Union contract terms will not change.

Getting bigger

“Bigger does not mean better in and of itself, but here it demonstrably does,” Blue said.

“Larger scale here translates into increased availability of capital at the lowest reasonable cost. Bigger in this instance also means greater supply chain leverage, enhanced operational experience, and industry-leading operating efficiency, all of which can drive further customer benefits,” he said.

Dominion expects its corporate credit rating to rise from BBB+ to A- at Standard & Poors, from Baa2 to Baa1 at Moody’s and from BBB+ to A- at Fitch. Dominion Energy Virginia is also expected to receive a one-notch upgrade at S&P, from BBB+ to A-.

Currently, that’s a 0.2 percentage point difference in interest rates when borrowing long-term money, according to debt markets data tracked by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis.

That may not sound like much, but on projects like the more than $2 billion Dominion plans to spend on transmission projects this year, it would translate to a nearly $2 million a year in savings on its borrowings if the company finances these projects with its usual mix of debt and equity, a Richmond Times-Dispatch analysis suggests.

Dominion’s debt costs flow directly to ratepayers.

Being bigger also means savings when buying material — from transformers to solar panels to gas turbines to power poles.

“Buying 100,000 widgets versus 25,000 widgets will produce more favorable pricing and better terms and conditions due to the size of the larger combined company’s buying power as compared to a smaller standalone company,” Ketchum said.

“Our industry is facing constraints in transformers, breakers, conductors, poles, meters, turbines, inverters, batteries, and other critical equipment. A company with larger procurement volumes, combined visibility into future needs, and broader supplier relationships is better positioned to manage cost and schedule pressure and ensure project execution is on time and on budget,” he said.

Those costs, too, are what ratepayers must cover with their monthly bills.

NextEra’s view

“The electric utility industry is at an inflection point. Demand for electricity is increasing, the resource adequacy challenge is becoming more complex, the generation mix is evolving, the transmission system must expand, and customers quite properly expect reliable service at costs that remain reasonable,” Ketchum said.

“Dominion and NextEra are at the apex of this growth. Both companies need more generation, transmission, and distribution infrastructure to meet increased demand for power. Both value enhanced resilience. Both are evaluating new nuclear and are deploying more renewables, more storage and ‘all of the above’ solutions that drive affordability and reliability over time,” he said.

“The point is to have the scale to buy, build, finance and operate more efficiently so that a utility can meet growing needs at the lowest reasonable cost over time,” he said.

Dominion Energy Virginia’s utility operations, transmission planning, distribution operations, regulatory affairs, governmental affairs, grid modernization, system planning, transmission engineering, storm response coordination, environmental services, customer operations, and energy policy stay in Richmond, Ketchum said.

“In short, the Dominion utilities will be operated locally out of Virginia just as they are today,” he said.

“And we won’t stop there. We will also look for opportunities to expand the combined company’s presence in Richmond through this combination,” he said.

title: The Next India-China Contest Will Be Fought Over Lithium, Not Ladakh
description:
China understood the strategic importance of critical minerals long before other major economies.
The integration provides Beijing with great leverage over global clean energy supply chains.
Recent export restrictions on gallium, germanium, and certain rare-earth technologies demonstrate that critical minerals, like oil, can serve as a strategic weapon.
Increasingly, critical minerals are seen as an important pillar of economic diplomacy, not a mining concern.
Critical minerals will be the geopolitics of the clean energy era.
text:
The International Energy Agency projects that under ambitious clean-energy scenarios, the demand for essential minerals could more than triple by 2040. The challenge is not simply resource availability but also processing capability, unlike oil. Here, China has been stealthily building one of the greatest strategic advantages of modern times. China understood the strategic importance of critical minerals long before other major economies. Rather than focus on domestic reserves, Beijing has invested throughout the entire value chain from overseas mining and refining of raw materials to making batteries, electric cars, and renewable technology. Chinese companies now dominate lithium refining, cobalt processing, and rare earth separation, along with a large chunk of the global battery manufacturing industry. Higher state investment, favorable industrial policy, and overseas acquisitions in Africa, Latin America, and Australia have helped companies such as CATL and BYD become global industrial giants. China’s edge is not in having the most deposits but in having the industrial ecosystem to turn raw minerals into high-value products. The integration provides Beijing with great leverage over global clean energy supply chains. Recent export restrictions on gallium, germanium, and certain rare-earth technologies demonstrate that critical minerals, like oil, can serve as a strategic weapon. This poses a major risk for India. The government has set a target of 500 GW of non-fossil fuel capacity by 2030, promoted electric transportation, manufactured green hydrogen, and emerged as a global manufacturing hub. These goals will require huge amounts of battery materials, but India is still heavily import-dependent for many of these critical inputs.

Open Magazine Latest Edition is Out Now!

The Second Life of Sanskrit

10 Jul 2026 - Vol 05 | Issue 28

Being classical has become cool

Read Now The Second Life of Sanskrit

The discovery of lithium resources in Jammu and Kashmir raised hopes that India may cut its import dependence. But the discoveries in geology do not automatically translate into strategic autonomy. Commercial extraction takes a year of exploration, environmental approvals, infrastructure development, and processing facilities. Even if local production becomes economically viable, India’s reserves are unlikely to be able to meet future demand. Additionally, lithium is only one piece of a much larger supply chain. Renewable technologies use rare earth metals in permanent magnets and wind turbines, and batteries require graphite, cobalt, nickel, manganese, and some specialized chemical processing. Resource finds are of little strategic value without domestic refining capacity and manufacturing ecosystems. India has tried to recalibrate its foreign policy in the light of these issues, vis-à-vis resource security. This is a major change: the establishment of Khanij Bidesh India Limited (KABIL), becoming an observer in the Minerals Security Partnership, MoUs with Australia on critical minerals, and increased interaction with Argentina, Chile, and African producers. Increasingly, critical minerals are seen as an important pillar of economic diplomacy, not a mining concern.

This is a sign of a broader change in world geopolitics. Resource-rich areas such as Africa's and Latin America’s so-called “Lithium Triangle” of Argentina, Bolivia, and Chile have become arenas of strategic competition. Over the last 20 years, China has invested heavily in these places: in infrastructure, in mining contracts, and in industry. Western countries worried about dependence on Chinese supply chains are acting with efforts including the US-led Minerals Security Partnership and the European Union’s Critical Raw Materials Act. India is late to the race, but with a huge advantage. Its democratic institutions, growing manufacturing base, and increasing partnerships with the likes of Australia, Japan, the United States, and France hold the potential to diversify and build resilient supply chains. The Quad, which was originally focused on maritime security, is now broadening its cooperation to cover technology, semiconductors, and supply chain resilience, all of which are directly connected to critical minerals. Buying assets in mining abroad will not be enough to fix India’s predicament. China's dominance wasn't simply about buying mines. It was built on long-term investment in refining technology, battery chemistry, logistics, manufacturing, and research. The real geopolitical asset is not the mineral itself but the industrial ability to transform into strategic products. Hence, India needs a holistic critical mineral policy that is more than just exploitation. Investment in improving infrastructure, battery recycling, better materials science, and alternative technologies such as sodium-ion batteries might help to ease future vulnerabilities. A circular economy that recovers precious minerals from end-of-life batteries and electronic waste is also key, which can reduce dependence on imported raw materials.

It is also important to consider the environmental dimension. The scramble for vital minerals could be about to echo the exploitative politics of the fossil fuel age. Mining projects often fuel fears about losing biodiversity, water scarcity, and indigenous rights. If the clean-energy transition just shifts environmental costs from oil-producing regions to mineral-abundant locations, it threatens to undermine its own sustainability aims. As India seeks to distinguish itself from cutthroat resource-based competition, it should emphasize responsible mining and open government in its international engagement. The fallout is more than economic. Advanced batteries, rare earth magnets, and specialist electronic components are becoming ever more important in defense technology. Artificial intelligence infrastructure requires reliable electricity systems with battery backup. Renewable energy adoption, electric mobility, and digital infrastructure are all interconnected aspects of national security. In this case, supply-chain resilience is no longer an industrial policy issue but a strategic requirement. The India-China rivalry would likely continue along the Line of Actual Control. Territorial issues remain unresolved, and military competition will likely continue. But to concentrate just on the Himalayas might be to miss the bigger transformation that’s taking place. In the coming decades, the balance of power will be influenced not only by military strength but also by technological dominance, industrial robustness, and mastery over the resources that fuel both.

Every era has its strategic resource in history. Coal was the fuel for the industrial revolution. The twentieth century was the century of oil. Critical minerals will be the geopolitics of the clean energy era. The nations that develop robust supply chains and sophisticated manufacturing systems and break away from strategic dependencies will shape the future of global economic leadership. That means India has a challenge that is more than matching China dollar for dollar in its mine investments. This is about building an integrated ecosystem that ties together mineral diplomacy, industrial policy, technological innovation, and strategic relationships. The next phase of the geopolitical struggle will be less about controlling discrete resources and more about dominating the industries they enable.

The confrontation between India and China will continue to be seen in the mountains of Ladakh. But the deeper battle for influence, prosperity, and strategic autonomy may be fought far from the Himalayas in labs developing next-generation batteries, refineries processing lithium, ports shipping critical minerals across the oceans, and diplomatic corridors where tomorrow’s energy alliances are being forged. The road to geopolitical dominance in an era of clean energy doesn’t only lie in contested borders but also in the minerals that will power the future of the world.

text:
Nuclear plants. Shipyards. Robots. Oil and gas.

Trying to connect the dots? You and I may not be able to, but Constellation Energy (NASDAQ:CEG) is doing just that with its latest power move.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Constellation, the largest nuclear energy company in the U.S., has invested an undisclosed sum in Blue Energy, a start-up specializing in prefabricated nuclear power plants. The real kicker isn't the tech – how this newcomer builds those plants is where the disruption lies, and exactly why Constellation decided it's worth the bet.

Image source: Getty Images.

Playing the nuclear energy boom

Constellation Energy is the undisputed clean energy leader in the U.S., operating the nation's largest nuclear fleet. That dominance has thrown the company straight into the spotlight of the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure boom.

Data centers consume staggering amounts of electricity, and they require uninterrupted, 24/7 power to keep their servers and cooling systems running. While solar and wind are intermittent, nuclear isn't.

The macro tailwinds are stronger than ever, with the U.S. government planning to quadruple domestic nuclear capacity by 2050. The problem is execution. Building a traditional nuclear reactor can easily take over a decade and tens of billions of dollars.

Blue Energy directly tackles the industry's two biggest bottlenecks: speed and financing. Their solution? Shipyards.

Why CEG thinks a shipyard can fit the nuclear equation

The biggest budget-killer in a nuclear power plant isn't the reactor itself. It is the buildings, structures, pipes, and cooling systems that can cause the maximum delays and cost overruns.

Shipyards already have mass assembly-line manufacturing processes in place. They also have the indoor, weather-controlled spaces, high-capacity cranes, and automated robotic set-ups designed for steel ships and offshore oil rigs.

text:
On July 19th, dozens of teams of high school students will begin a five-day, 630-mile road race from Fort Worth to Fort Stockton in Texas. But this is not your typical contest. The students design and build the cars themselves, using off-the-shelf parts and 3D printed materials. The winner is the team that accumulates the most driven miles. And the only fuel they can use to power their Frankenstein-looking vehicles comes from that mass of incandescent gas that hangs in our sky: the Sun.

This year is the 30th anniversary of the annual Solar Car Challenge, a contest that brings together high school students from around the country with the one goal to build the fastest, most efficient solar-powered car. The race was founded in 1993 by Dr. Lehman Marks, a Texas educator with a long-held interest in STEM. Students learn a variety of skills through the challenge, including project management, budgeting, fundraising, and engineering. But mostly, they have to build a race-worthy solar vehicle that can hopefully go the distance.

This year is the 30th anniversary of the annual Solar Car Challenge, a contest that brings together high school students from around the country with the one goal to build the solar-powered car that can go the distance

Lehman said that the Solar Car Challenge was born out of his frustration with the state of STEM education in the late ’80s and early ’90s. At the time, he had a group of students who were disengaged and uninspired by learning solely from textbooks, and seeking a way to spark their interest, he accepted an invitation from a friend at the University of North Texas, who was building a collegiate solar car for what was then a brand-new competition.

“We went up there and the kids were just mesmerized by the intricacy of the solar project,” he told me. “And all the way back from Desmond to Dallas, they kept yelling, ‘Doc, won’t you please let us build a solar car?’”

He relented, but quickly realized that high school students would never be able to compete fairly against college teams because they lacked the technical expertise and financial resources available to universities. Thus, the Solar Car Challenge for high school students was born, with the educational program officially kicking off in 1993 and the first national competition in 1995.

Since its inception, the program has engaged over 85,000 students across 39 states and multiple countries, including Canada, Mexico, Costa Rica, Spain, and Singapore. There are currently over 260 active high school solar projects. The event alternates formats between on-track and cross-country, with this year’s event being a grueling, 630-mile race across Texas. The five-day trek starts July 19th in Fort Worth and travels through the towns of Palestine, Round Rock, Fredericksburg, and San Angelo, before finishing in Fort Stockton. Lehman said that town residents come out and celebrate the teams each time they pass through.

”It’s not just building a car,” Lehman stressed. “It’s learning how to officially drive that car. In this coming event, one of the things I’ve been preaching to the kids is, before you ever get here, you need to put 500 miles in your car. You need to know, will it break? You need to know, even if it breaks, let it break in your own parking lot so you can fix it.”

The race typically features three categories of competition: classic, advanced, and electric-solar power, in which the teams race electric vehicles that receive energy from stationary solar power stations. This year’s challenge introduces a new division: cruiser. In this category, teams build four-seater vehicles with solar arrays integrated directly into the car’s body.

The decision to create a new division was born out of years of people questioning whether solar cars would ever resemble actual automobiles instead of flat, highly aerodynamic vehicles with a driver often crammed beneath a wide solar panel. Indeed, many of the cars barely resemble anything you would recognize as road-worthy, appearing more like a mix between futuristic spacecraft and high-tech go-karts.

“It’s not just building a car.”

— Lehman Marks, Founder of the Solar Car Challenge

Lehman said the organizers wanted students to build solar-powered vehicles that looked like real passenger cars, with solar cells integrated into the bodywork itself, room for four passengers, four doors, and a trunk. He believes this helps demonstrate that solar-powered transportation can have practical applications, allowing people to imagine what future solar-assisted passenger vehicles might actually look like.

“People would say, ‘Oh, this is really neat, but it’s not reality,’” he said. “Now we can show them what it could be. And I think that’s a step up.”

Blake Wood is a 17-year-old rising senior from Benbrook Middle-High School in a suburb of Fort Worth. He’s also one of the captains of the Old Rip Racing solar car team, one of the few independent teams in the race. Their 14-member team includes students from three different schools, something Wood sees as their biggest strength, because it allows students who otherwise would never have met to collaborate on a shared engineering challenge.

Wood says the team began planning approximately a year before the competition. Their earliest work consisted of paper sketches while they studied successful cars from previous years in the Classic Division, which is intended primarily for first- and second-year teams. They analyzed what made those other cars work well and incorporated those ideas into their own initial concepts. As the project progressed, the team improved its computer-aided design (CAD) skills, gradually translating their hand-drawn concepts into digital engineering models. Learning the design software became part of the educational process.

“People would say, ‘Oh, this is really neat, but it’s not reality.’”

— Lehman Marks

“I think our vehicle, it looks really nice to me,” Wood tells me. “It’s unfortunate. So we don’t really get to see it that often all put together, and it feels like we’re always fixing something or making something and then putting something back on, and then we’re like, ‘Oh no, we need to weld in that area. Let’s take that electrical component back off.’”

But while battery-electric vehicles have become mainstream, solar cars have remained largely experimental. A number of startups pursuing solar cars have either pivoted to more proven technology or gone bankrupt. Wood says he’s optimistic that solar vehicles have real long-term potential, as long as educational competitions like the Solar Car Challenge continue to expose students to renewable energy technologies at an early age. As participants eventually enter professional careers, they can continue developing the innovations needed to make solar transportation commercially viable.

“We’re making progress,” Wood said. “I mean, we have a whole lot of high school students making them, and I think with the right equipment and a little more expertise than maybe all of us have, I think it could definitely be possible.”

Lehman agrees, pointing to startups like Aptera that are still pursuing the goal of a mass-market solar car. But he said that commercialization has never been the real goal of the Solar Car Challenge.

“People say, ‘Well, are you trying to build a better solar car?’ Between you and me, I’m not,” he said. “I’m trying to build a student who is capable, who learns about commitment, dedication to a project, to learn about teamwork, to learn about engineering and battery technology. I’m trying to build a workforce and trying to build engineers.”

title: From Black Gold to Critical Minerals: The New Strategic Shift in Global Geopolitics
description:
Nations with influence over these strategic resources possessed the power to shape international politics and the global economy.
While oil remains an essential energy source, its exclusive strategic dominance is gradually giving way to a new set of resources: critical minerals.
In contrast, China dominates the production and processing of critical minerals.
China’s Fifteenth Five-Year Plan (2026–2030) further reinforces this strategy by identifying critical minerals as a core element of national security.
The move triggered serious concerns within Washington, particularly because advanced U.S. defense systems, including the F-35 fighter jet, rely heavily on Chinese critical minerals.
text:
The greatest geopolitical contest of the twentieth century revolved around “black gold”—crude oil. For more than a century, the global order was shaped by those who controlled oil fields, pipelines, and key maritime chokepoints. Nations with influence over these strategic resources possessed the power to shape international politics and the global economy.

Today, however, the geopolitical landscape is undergoing a profound transformation. While oil remains an essential energy source, its exclusive strategic dominance is gradually giving way to a new set of resources: critical minerals. Lithium, cobalt, nickel, graphite, and rare earth elements (REEs) have become the strategic assets of the twenty-first century. These minerals are no longer just industrial commodities; they are the foundation of modern technology, clean energy, and national security.

History teaches us that the Stone Age did not end because the world ran out of stone. Likewise, the changing importance of hydrocarbons is not driven by oil shortages but by the rapid evolution of global industries. Electric vehicles (EVs), renewable energy systems, semiconductors, and advanced defense technologies now depend heavily on mineral-based supply chains rather than traditional fossil fuels.

According to recent reports by the International Energy Agency (IEA), global demand for critical minerals is expected to increase sixfold in the coming years if countries are to achieve their clean energy and climate goals.

Unlike oil, however, the supply chain for critical minerals is highly concentrated. Oil reserves are distributed across several major producers, including Saudi Arabia, Russia, the United States, and Gulf nations. In contrast, China dominates the production and processing of critical minerals. It currently accounts for around 70 percent of global rare earth production and more than 85 percent of refining capacity. China also controls nearly 80 percent of global lithium processing and virtually all battery-grade graphite production.

The real geopolitical battle is not over mining itself but over refining technology. Raw minerals can be extracted from different parts of the world, but transforming them into materials suitable for batteries, electronics, and advanced manufacturing largely depends on Chinese processing capabilities.

Beijing laid the foundations of this dominance decades ago. While many Western countries remained focused on oil politics in the Middle East, China quietly expanded its influence across Africa and Latin America under its “Go Out” strategy launched in 1999. Today, China controls not only mineral extraction but also the entire value chain—from mining and refining to battery manufacturing and electric vehicle production.

China’s Fifteenth Five-Year Plan (2026–2030) further reinforces this strategy by identifying critical minerals as a core element of national security. Beijing aims to become the world’s leading supplier of battery-grade minerals by 2035.

The United States has become increasingly aware of this strategic dependency. After the second Trump administration took office in 2025 and trade tensions with China intensified, Beijing imposed export restrictions on several rare earth minerals. The move triggered serious concerns within Washington, particularly because advanced U.S. defense systems, including the F-35 fighter jet, rely heavily on Chinese critical minerals.

In response, the United States has launched multi-billion-dollar investment programs to build strategic mineral stockpiles and diversify supply chains. Washington is strengthening partnerships with countries such as Australia, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Japan, and Ukraine to reduce reliance on Chinese-controlled resources.

This global competition has also enhanced the strategic importance of resource-rich developing nations. The Democratic Republic of Congo produces nearly 70 percent of the world’s cobalt, while Indonesia controls approximately half of global nickel production. These countries are increasingly demanding greater local processing and industrial development instead of merely exporting raw materials.

Indonesia has even proposed the idea of an OPEC-style organization for nickel-producing nations, reflecting the rise of resource nationalism. Although technological changes in battery chemistry and geopolitical challenges may complicate such initiatives, mineral-rich countries are determined to secure greater economic benefits from their natural resources.

Unlike the geopolitical conflicts of the past, the new “critical minerals cold war” is being fought less with military force and more through tariffs, sanctions, export controls, and technological competition. Economic coercion has become one of the defining features of this emerging rivalry.

At the same time, illegal mining has become an increasing source of funding for armed groups and criminal networks. Rebel organizations in the Democratic Republic of Congo and insurgent groups in parts of Latin America continue to exploit valuable minerals such as tungsten and tantalum to finance conflict and instability.

Looking ahead, the rise of critical minerals will not eliminate the importance of traditional energy resources, but it will create a far more complex geopolitical environment. No single country is likely to dominate the entire global supply chain indefinitely. However, those nations that successfully build complete value chains—from mining and refining to advanced manufacturing—will gain significant economic and strategic advantages.

The most important lesson of this new mineral era is clear. Countries that merely export raw materials will remain economically dependent on others. Those that invest in processing industries, refineries, manufacturing facilities, and technological innovation will be better positioned to safeguard their economic sovereignty and strategic independence

text:
Cindy Case-Brown and Connie Norris sit on the far side of the nearly empty hearing room in the Galvez Building in Baton Rouge, several small stacks of documents and binders spread out before them. Across the room sit representatives from the Louisiana Public Service Commission and Magnolia Water, accompanied by a squadron of attorneys.

The two Magnolia customers traveled from the Northshore to the state capital to oppose a plan that would allow the private equity-backed company to continue to increase water and sewer rates annually. In recent years, Magnolia has bought up utility systems across the state, becoming one of Louisiana’s largest water and sewer providers.

Like many Louisiana residents, Case-Brown and Norris have seen their utility rates soar since Magnolia took over their local system. Unlike most, they dove headfirst into the regulatory muck.

It has been an uphill battle since day one.

“I had very little knowledge of what was going on and how the system worked,” says Norris, who eventually became an intervenor in one of Magnolia’s repeated requests to the LPSC for permission to raise its rates on customers like herself.

The process is similar to court proceedings — only Norris and fellow Magnolia customers don’t have anyone to represent them but themselves.

According to LPSC records, Magnolia now provides sewer to more than 82,000 customers across the state and water to an additional 79,000 connections. The company continues to expand through acquisitions.

Since Magnolia started expanding in 2019, the company has increased utility rates for its customers nearly every year, making its sewer rates the highest in the state. Residents in Lafayette’s Quail Hollow neighborhood saw sewer rate hikes as high as 200%. Most customers now pay more than $73 a month for sewer service, along with a starting water rate of $44. By comparison, the statewide average is $56 for sewer service and a $19 starting water rate.

Fighting those increases, as Case-Brown and Norris set out to do, is difficult.

The LPSC, the state body in charge of regulating and approving rate increases by private companies like Magnolia, has a tendency to approve them without much discussion, in part because it sees its role as ensuring that those companies have the financial wherewithal to continue operations and comply with federal and state regulations.

“The LPSC is responsible for ensuring that utilities are able to generate enough funds to maintain compliance with these regulatory agencies,” writes LPSC staff in its Magnolia hearing filings.

Meanwhile, Magnolia has done everything in its power to make intervention as painful as possible, arguing that ratepayers like Case-Brown and Norris should have to sign non-disclosure agreements to see the financial data the company used to justify its rate increases, and even requesting insight into their personal finances and medical records in return.

Magnolia did not respond to any requests for comment by The Current for this story. All quotes from Magnolia representatives come from public hearings and filings.

The company argues it needs to raise rates in order to fix the many old systems it has taken over that had fallen into disrepair under previous ownership.

Higher operating costs, shrinking populations and lack of government support have left many small towns with failing systems and no money to hire engineers to fix the deficiencies.

According to a 2020 report from the American Society of Civil Engineers, spending on capital improvements to water infrastructure in 2019 at the local, state and federal levels totaled only $48 billion.

This fell $81 billion short of the $129 billion ASCE estimates is needed to effectively modernize the system. At the same time, ASCE gave water systems across the country a D rating, meaning improvements are needed for failing systems now.

Those are exactly the kinds of systems Magnolia and its parent company have taken over in Louisiana and beyond.

Like the water system serving the town of Kilian, Louisiana, which is among the for-profit utility provider’s most recent acquisitions.

Until 2026, the town’s water system consistently received a D or F rating from the Louisiana Department of Health.

The town tried, and failed, to drag itself out. “We were going to go bankrupt. Hiring these engineering firms or these contractors is incredibly expensive,” says Mayor Caleb Atwell of the repairs needed to keep Killian’s water drinkable.

Manganese and iron concentrations are high in the area’s groundwater, and improper filtration makes the water coming out of the tap less than appetizing.

“You’re turning on your sink, and it looks like gumbo is coming out,” says Atwell. “And not the good kind of gumbo. We’re talking tomato.”

Atwell was elected mayor in 2025. By that time, the town’s water system had already been in receivership, meaning the state had taken ownership of the system due to the persistently bad ratings. Meanwhile, residents paid less than $30 for water service a month, nowhere near enough to generate the funds for necessary repairs, he argues.

“People really don’t care too much about the pipes that are in the ground, until they start breaking,” says Atwell. “You’re only charging people $28 a month, great, but you can’t put in the dollars that it takes to upgrade.”

After over a year in receivership, the Louisiana Department of Health came to Killian with an ultimatum: Sell the system to Magnolia or fight the court-ordered sale of the system.

“We really didn’t have an option but to go with Magnolia,” says Atwell.

Magnolia Founder and CEO Josiah Cox agrees. “I believe we’re the only entity that’s kind of capable or willing to step into that situation,” he told the LPSC in a February hearing.

But unlike a public utility like Lafayette Utilities System and many of the water and sewage districts it takes over, Magnolia is backed by private investors and expected to turn a profit for those shareholders.

Magnolia’s most recent rate plan approved by the LPSC ensures customer rates provide a 9% to 10% financial return for Magnolia, on top of the tens of millions in expenses the company already recoups from acquiring and operating systems.

According to its application for rate increases in 2025, Magnolia owed more than $37.5 million to its parent company, funds that have been used to support the company’s expansion across the state. Continued expansion, Cox argues, is necessary for the company’s business model to function, something he says will bring down rates in the long run.

“We can buy equipment that smaller utilities couldn’t afford on their own, because we’re managing multiple utilities across a larger footprint,” Cox said in the February hearing.

Assessing the validity of that claim and arguing against it, if necessary, requires a level of expertise that many ratepayers — and even regulators — lack, says Jackson Voss, a law student working for the Alliance for Affordable Energy, a nonprofit that intervenes in electrical rate cases on behalf of ratepayers.

“Doing that requires very active regulation and very active balancing of the interests involved,” says Voss. “And that’s not something that [the public services commission] does a good job of.”

Part of that is due to a lack of experience with water and sewer systems in general, many of which had so far been managed on the local level.

“The LPSC has not had a super long history of dealing with private water companies,” says Voss. “Water is not their primary focus. It was railroad monopolies … now it’s become electricity.”

As for ratepayers, if they lived in another state, there may be a state-funded advocate helping them pursue fair regulation of their rates. Louisiana is one of only a handful of states that don’t offer such representation.

“It’s a pretty bad time, in my view, to be a customer in Louisiana who’s hoping that the LPSC is going to protect them from what these companies want to do to them,” Voss says.

Case-Brown and Norris’ attempt to fight the rate increases on their Magnolia-issued bills failed. In June, the LPSC approved the company’s rate plan for the next three years.

But their fight, along with an increase of ratepayers across the state who find themselves in a similar situation, has brought unprecedented attention to the issue.

Magnolia will now be subject to an audit of its operating company’s finances before applying for another rate increase, ordered by the judge in Case-Brown and Norris’ intervention proceedings.

There’s also an election for the commission seat representing their area, and several candidates have made Magnolia a central part of their campaign. Norris herself is running.

Her opponent, following a recent runoff election, state Rep. Stephanie Hilferty, R-Metairie, called on the commission to stop any new rate hikes or acquisitions by Magnolia. “The residents that have Magnolia Water cannot deal with another ‘moderate’ rate hike,” she told the sitting commissioners this June.

Case-Brown, who lives in Mandeville, is proud of the work she and fellow Northshore ratepayers like Norris have done to call attention to an issue few understood or were aware of before, and against an opponent that seemed to have all the power on its side.

“We stood up to a bully and I’m proud of that,” she tells The Current. “More people need to do the same.”

text:
Electric vehicle giant Tesla plans to boost production at its factory near Berlin in the 2026 financial year as demand recovers and profits improve, according to the company's annual report for its German manufacturing unit.

The company forecasts a significant increase in production volume compared with the previous year, Tesla Manufacturing Brandenburg SE said in its 2025 annual report.

It said capacity utilization was also expected to rise and that the plant would supply more than 30 markets while expanding into additional ones.

Tesla earlier this year said it aimed to increase output at Gruenheide to as many as 7,500 vehicles a week, or about 375,000 a year, while expanding battery cell production.

The company plans to create 3,500 new jobs and says it aims to integrate the entire value chain from battery cells to finished vehicles at the site.

Tesla said the expansion remained subject to economic conditions and warned that escalating geopolitical tensions and potential supply chain disruptions could affect its outlook.

It also said plans for full battery cell production at Grennheide depended on market conditions, citing challenges facing battery manufacturing in Europe compared to the U.S. and China.

The German unit reported net profit of 77.1 million euros ($88.2 million) for 2025, up by about 20 million euros from the previous year, despite what it described as a challenging market environment.

Revenue fell to 7.1 billion euros from 7.7 billion euros in 2024, while vehicle production declined to about 202,000 units from around 211,000. Tesla attributed the drop mainly to a model changeover and the introduction of new variants, adding that production remained stable overall.

The Gruenheide factory, Tesla's only European production site, opened in March 2022 and currently produces the Model Y. It employed about 11,000 people, including temporary workers, at the end of 2025, according to the report.

text:
Global investment in critical minerals declined by 9 per cent in 2025, ending several years of growth despite strong long-term demand for minerals essential to clean energy technologies, electric vehicles and advanced industries, according to the International Energy Agency's (IEA) Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026.

The report attributed the slowdown to rising geopolitical tensions, price volatility and a more cautious investment environment, even as demand fundamentals remained strong.

"Critical mineral investment declined by 9 per cent in 2025, ending several years of growth. Amid rising geopolitical tensions and price volatility, investors became more cautious despite strong underlying demand," the report said.

Advt

Battery metals witnessed the steepest pullback in investment. According to the report, capital spending in the segment fell by more than 20 per cent, marking the sharpest decline in over a decade, while lithium companies cut investment by around 40 per cent.

In contrast, copper continued to attract capital, with spending by copper-focused companies increasing 8 per cent, reflecting confidence in the metal's long-term demand outlook, the report added.

The IEA said exploration spending also weakened, declining by more than 10 per cent in 2025. Spending on lithium and nickel exploration dropped by around 45 per cent, outweighing steady investment in copper and modest growth in uranium exploration. Most regions recorded lower exploration budgets, although Asia Pacific stood out with a 20 per cent increase.

Despite weaker private investment, governments stepped up financial support for critical mineral projects.

"Public finance commitments in advanced economies reached around USD 65 billion in 2025, over four times higher than in 2023," the report said, adding that a significant gap still remains between announced commitments and actual disbursements, which will determine how much these measures help diversify supply chains.

The report also found that investment across the critical minerals value chain remains uneven. While mining projects continue to move ahead, refining and downstream processing capacity are not keeping pace.

Advt

"Analysis of project pipelines reveals a structural imbalance in efforts to promote supply chain diversification, with refining and downstream capacity lagging behind mining," the IEA said. It noted that in battery materials, planned cathode production capacity amounts to only about one-third of projected lithium mining capacity, highlighting the need for more balanced investment across the supply chain.

The agency said governments are increasingly deploying policy support, including grants, concessional loans and equity participation, to reduce investment risks and mobilise private capital for strategically important mineral projects as countries seek to build more resilient and diversified supply chains.

text:
Turbine plan for 'Hockney Country' moves closer

A proposal to build six large wind turbines in the East Yorkshire Wolds has moved a step closer.

Formal plans have now been submitted to East Riding of Yorkshire Council for the Three Oaks Renewable Energy Park near to Burton Agnes, a landscape made famous by the late artist David Hockney.

The tip of each turbine will be 488ft (149m) high and concerns have been raised by local residents about the visual impact of the scheme.

However, developers Ridge Clean Energy said the project would have no adverse impact on the character of the wider landscape and would produce renewable electricity for 24,000 local homes.

It is one of the biggest onshore turbine proposals in England since the government lifted an effective ban two years ago.

The machines will tower over the local landscape but they will also come with what developers describe as a "community benefit fund" worth £5m over the 40-year life of the project.

Residents in nearby villages have previously expressed concerns about the plans, citing the potential for both visual and noise impacts.

Ridge Clean Energy said it would combine the turbines with an already approved solar farm and battery storage to "deliver an excellent source of secure and reliable renewable energy at a time when it is needed most", according to its website.

Detailed plans for the Three Oaks Renewable Energy Park have now been published on East Riding Council's planning portal, allowing for public consultation.

A spokesperson for Ridge Clean Energy said it had been working with communities local to the site over the past five years and said the project had been "sensitively designed following detailed technical work reviewing landscape and visual effects, biodiversity suitability and operational noise assessments".

"Our design has been prepared taking local consultation representations into account, as well as in line with the relevant planning guidance," the spokesperson added.

If the plans are approved by the council, construction work could begin in 2028.

And six states — Utah, Maryland, Colorado, New Hampshire, Virginia and Maine — have already passed laws allowing homeowners and renters to use plug-in solar systems.
In addition to displacing millions of metric tons of emissions every year, plug-in solar can ease strain on our electric grid.
Plug-in solar could also help address affordability and equity concerns, especially for those most burdened by surges in fossil fuel pricing.

text:
With retail electric bills rising 61% faster than inflation, more Americans are looking for ways to address their high energy bills. One obvious answer is solar, which is now the cheapest energy source in history. California lawmakers are currently considering a law, the Plug and Play Solar Act, that would allow many more residents, including renters, to take advantage of this technology and its cost-savings.

California Senate Bill 868, sponsored by Senator Scott Wiener, D-San Francisco, passed the Senate 35-1 and is now making its way through the Assembly. This bill would cut the red tape around plug-in solar — a system of portable panels that generate electricity and, through a connection to a standard home’s 120-volt outlet, channel it safely into a household’s wiring to power its appliances.

Without the Plug and Play Solar Act, the small 400-watt panels that these systems use, which are typically hung from balconies or put on patios, are treated as much larger solar arrays that require permits and approvals by utility companies.

If passed, the law will help millions bypass red tape to harness the power of the sun — no contractor, permitting or fussy install required. Estimates suggest that plug-in solar could save Americans $13 billion a year, all while offsetting thousands of megawatts of electricity demand, which is often otherwise met by burning more polluting coal, oil and natural gas.

California is in good company in its pursuit of affordable solar options. Bills that would make DIY solar easier to adopt have already been introduced, with bipartisan support, in over half of U.S. states. And six states — Utah, Maryland, Colorado, New Hampshire, Virginia and Maine — have already passed laws allowing homeowners and renters to use plug-in solar systems.

In addition to displacing millions of metric tons of emissions every year, plug-in solar can ease strain on our electric grid. California is facing skyrocketing demand for electricity thanks to data centers and the costs of cooling in ever-hotter summers. When gas prices go up or storms take down power lines, solar panels can keep essential appliances running.

Plug-in solar could also help address affordability and equity concerns, especially for those most burdened by surges in fossil fuel pricing. Today, 70% of Americans don’t have access to rooftop solar systems because we rent or otherwise can’t afford the steep costs of rooftop panels.

Black, Native American and Latino households spend more of their income on energy than white households do, but they, along with low-income households, are also more likely to rent than to own. That means that one option to meaningfully bring down the cost of electricity — rooftop solar — is unavailable to them. Plug-in solar, which offers annual household savings between $200 and $400 and doesn’t require any permanent structural changes, could help.

Most Americans prefer wind and solar to gas and oil. What’s getting in our way isn’t a lack of interest in clean energy; it’s regulations that wrongly treat small plug-in systems the same as much larger solar arrays. Plug-in panels are already popular internationally, where permits and installers aren’t required. Twenty-seven European countries have legalized plug-in solar. In Germany, around 3 million balcony solar kits are in use, and experts say they are demonstrably safe.

That hasn’t stopped utility companies from lobbying to block their use, citing possible safety hazards to customers and workers fixing power lines during outages. But safety measures are already part of California’s plug-in legislation, which requires testing and certification of devices to ensure that they will shut off automatically when the power goes out, protecting against circuit issues.

Of course, balcony solar isn’t going to solve all of our energy affordability issues, and the costs of even small panels — around $500 for an 800 watt system — may be a stretch for the 14 million Americans with utility debt. Still, passing plug-in solar legislation is a step in the right direction. It certainly doesn’t prevent us from taking further action to help the planet.

Changing state laws can drive the price of plug-in solar even lower. Market research predicts that if five or more states adopt plug-in solar, the cost of these systems will drop, and all the more so if one of those states is California, the largest solar market in the country.

Plug-in solar will reduce utility costs and advance more equitable access to clean energy at the same time.

title: Colorado academics grapple with fallout from Trump's research cuts - The Denver Post
description:

Information science students would learn how to become better science communicators.
But Fiesler was among the legion of academics whose research was halted last year by drastic federal funding cuts.

text:
Casey Fiesler suspects she wound up in the federal government’s crosshairs for attempting to combat misinformation.

The U.S. National Science Foundation awarded the University of Colorado Boulder information science professor a $268,428 grant in the fall of 2024. The funds were slated for a project teaming up CU media and communication students with information science students to create educational social media content about artificial intelligence.

Scholars well-versed in communication would learn more about the complicated nature of AI. Information science students would learn how to become better science communicators. And social media users would benefit from accurate, compelling information.

That was the goal.

But Fiesler was among the legion of academics whose research was halted last year by drastic federal funding cuts. The grant terminations stalled or stopped progress on scholarship that the Trump administration deemed out of alignment with its mission — largely, research surrounding diverse populations, misinformation and climate change.

“The project just died, and my assumption is the reason it got cut was the abstract had the word ‘misinformation’ in it,” Fiesler said. The Trump administration focused on canceling grants across the country researching the spread of misinformation and disinformation, stating this kind of research could infringe on protected speech rights.

In Colorado, more than $375 million in grants from the National Science Foundation, National Institutes of Health, U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention were disrupted — either terminated and reinstated through legal levers, or axed altogether — in the first 18 months of the Trump administration, according to the tracking project Grant Witness.

Some of the terminated grant money has since been reinstated, and some remains tied up in court, but Colorado academics say the damage is far-reaching beyond the individual grants. When federal money dried up, some schools let researchers go. Others chose to leave, unwilling or unable to deal with the months of financial uncertainty.

The loss in funding hurt researchers’ careers and stunted young scholars from entering the profession, experts say. But, in the bigger picture, the billions in rescinded research dollars across the nation blighted scientific progress and innovation for years to come, academics said.

“The U.S. has for a long time been a respected source of innovation in knowledge generation, and that’s what we’re losing,” said Lynn Schofield Clark, a professor at the University of Denver who lost a $150,000 grant last year. “That’s something we can’t get back.”

Getting ‘DOGE’d’

More than 170 grants were disrupted in 2025 among Colorado research institutions CU Boulder, DU, Colorado State University and the Colorado School of Mines, according to those schools.

At CU Boulder, a $1.2 million National Science Foundation grant intended to reduce racially biased beliefs through teaching human genetics in high school biology was axed. At CSU, a $6 million grant studying the growth of artificial joints to help osteoarthritis patients met its demise. At Mines, $105,000 toward increasing degree completion for underrepresented students in STEM was terminated.

DU’s Schofield Clark, a journalism and media studies professor, lost a grant from the National Endowment for the Humanities for her work incorporating local Chicano history into common curriculum classes at the university, so all students had the chance to learn Chicano history in general education courses.

“We wanted to see if we could look into resources and generate new resources and teach our students by enabling them to have direct contact with the cultural arts scene, the history scene and hear from people who had an impact on shaping this area,” Schofield Clark said.

The program, which reached about 350 DU students, kicked off in the spring semester of 2023. The grant funding allowed Schofield Clark to take DU students to local Chicano festivals, the History Colorado museum and music events, and to bring Chicano community members to campus to tell their stories directly to students.

It was going so well that last year, Schofield Clark and two of her graduate students went to a Chicano studies academic conference to present their work. At the conference, they learned their grant funding had been “DOGE’D,” as Schofield Clark and other researchers called the federal funding terminations.

The Department of Government Efficiency, or DOGE, was one of Trump’s first initiatives during his second term, initially spearheaded by Elon Musk. The initiative, which ended this month, stated its mission was “maximizing governmental efficiency and productivity.” The department is responsible for mass federal layoffs and the termination of more than 15,800 federal grants across agencies totaling about $49 billion, according to the DOGE website.

Many of those terminations targeted grants associated with marginalized populations — like researching how a new drug might affect women or how to better recruit and retain students of color in science programs.

Schofield Clark’s vision of bringing the Chicano community to DU students put a target on her back. The professor recalled receiving a termination letter from the federal government with a “very insulting” tone similar to “we are rescinding this grant and giving it to people who are more worthy,” she said.

“That definitely derailed things,” Schofield Clark said.

The program slowed. The university funded what it could, Schofield Clark said.

At DU, 21 grants were terminated under the Trump administration, though all but five have been reinstated, said Corinne Lengsfeld, the university’s vice provost for research and graduate education.

Still, Lengsfeld said research expenditures at the university have decreased “significantly,” about 20%, during Trump’s second term, as faculty continue to face long delays in federal grant approvals and ongoing uncertainty.

“Because of all this, we are not going to be a top, intellectually rich country soon, and that is concerning,” Lengsfeld said.

Schofield Clark’s grant could now be reinstated.

After losing in court following the agency’s termination of more than 1,400 grants, the National Endowment for the Humanities started offering terminated grant recipients the option to reinstate those dollars this month.

Schofield Clark hopes to receive the rest of her funding and continue the work. She wants to share her history curriculum with other universities so they can implement similar programs — a step she wasn’t able to take after the funding loss.

While her own funding loss was frustrating, Schofield Clark noted broader implications. Within the past decade, she said, researchers have contended with the reality that so much academic scholarship has advanced through a white, Western lens.

“We’ve had a lot of knowledge gaps, and we need to address those because that’s part of who we are as a country,” Schofield Clark said. “This was a major disruption and a major slap in the face for a large population of people who have every right to have more knowledge about their history and health and everything.”

‘The disruptions have been real’

Full grant terminations have not been the only hit to academic research under the Trump administration.

Rescinded grants that ultimately were reinstated through court challenges left universities in limbo long enough to either force them to lay off researchers or cause frustrated faculty to quit or go elsewhere, said Cass Moseley, CSU’s vice president for research.

“A lot of faculty are trying to either pivot to slightly adjacent work that’s maybe more fundable for the federal government or seeking non-federal sources, although we know non-federal funding cannot replace federal money,” Moseley said.

CSU saw nearly 70 grants disrupted since last year, totaling more than $84 million, according to university tracking. Many of those were climate-related or tied to diversity, equity, and inclusion, Moseley said.

Even so, Moseley said there are huge delays in grant approvals and more complicated processes to apply for and receive federal funding, straining a nation that was once a thriving research enterprise.

“The disruptions have been real,” said Massimo Ruzzene, CU Boulder’s vice chancellor of research and innovation.

Ruzzene is worried about the hit to workforce development. Young academics just starting their research careers were seeing their work halted by funding cuts before they even got started, Ruzzene said.

“This impacts the training of a new generation of scientists and scholars,” Ruzzene said.

Postdoctoral scholar Alice Taylor was thrilled to be hired to work on a DU project researching anti-authoritarian movements led by women and LGBTQ+ activists worldwide.

In April of 2025, the $486,000 National Science Foundation grant that funded Taylor’s position was terminated, and the emerging scholar was left scrambling to pay rent.

“There’s a reason why authoritarian regimes go after universities first,” Taylor said. “What’s happened with Trump and DOGE is straight from authoritarian playbooks. Universities have the potential to stand up and be leaders and defend what universities are best at: freedom of speech, having robust faculty unions, high-quality, critical education.”

A new threat

The Trump administration is trying to assert even more control over academic research as the White House Office of Management and Budget proposes overhauling the Uniform Guidance for Federal Financial Assistance — a framework governing how federal agencies administer funds.

Colorado academics, along with universities across the nation, spoke of the overhaul in cataclysmic terms, noting the proposed guidelines would politicize research and innovation in a way that would be hard to pull back.

The proposal would authorize federal agencies to change or cut awards based on shifting presidential priorities and take away existing appeals processes, academic experts said.

“Those terms and conditions reflect the president’s agenda in some ways that are quite hard for universities,” Moseley said.

The ⁠Trump administration said the changes are intended to improve transparency, accountability and oversight for federal grants.

Meanwhile, the American Association for Cancer Research said the “harmful” proposal would be “extremely disruptive to the lifesaving research that the federal government funds and oversees.”

These overarching observations about the federal government’s impact on life-saving, innovative, revolutionary academic research are what most concerned the Colorado academics who spoke to The Denver Post.

“The loss in funding, of course, will have immediate operational impacts for students and researchers,” Ruzzene said. “It will also have scientific impacts as researchers cannot do their work. It will have workforce impacts. There will be less innovation — less products, less patents, less industry partnerships. This erosion will be difficult and take a long time to rebuild. That will have an impact on our ability to be prosperous economically as a nation, to fund careers for our children, to have scientific progress.”

“While we are in challenging times, we need to keep focus on what we do best, which is creating knowledge and transferring that knowledge to our students,” Ruzzene said.

title: Iberdrola, a global leader in electrification. - TIME
description:
At COP29 last year, leaders and stakeholders confronted this challenge head-on, setting ambitious goals to reshape the global energy landscape.
